# Builtins

No `import` is needed; builtins are resolved by name. The libc-backed ones may
also be imported from a `nish:` module, which is the same builtin under a name
that cannot be shadowed (see [Builtin modules](#builtin-modules-nish) below).
Effects (`none`, `read`, `write`) are what the call does to the purity of the
enclosing function
([ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#attribute-soundness-rules)).

## Builtin modules (`nish:`)

The builtins backed by the C runtime can be imported instead of reached for as
globals. `nish:` is the only bare specifier the language accepts; but for
`nish:secret` and `nish:region`, which have source behind them
([Secrets](#secrets-nishsecret), [Regions](#regions-nishregion)), it
resolves to no file, and the import *renames a builtin rather than introducing one* —
the call checks through the same rule and emits the same IR as the global
spelling, which `tests/run.js` pins by compiling `tests/cases/io_nish_import`
and `io_nish_import_global` and comparing the two bodies.

| Module | Exports |
| --- | --- |
| [`nish:fs`](../nish-fs.md) | `readFileSync`, `readFileSyncOrNull`, `readFileBytesSync`, `writeFileSync`, `appendFileSync`, `writeFileBytesSync`, `renameSync`, `unlinkSync`, `writeFileSyncMode`, `createFileExclusiveSync`, `mkdirSync`, `mkdirSyncMode`, `isDirectorySync`, `readdirSync`, `realpathSync`, `statMtimeSync` |
| [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md) | `exit` (the global `process.exit`), `getenv`, `spawnSync`, `spawnSyncTo`, `spawnPiped`, `spawn`, `spawnWithFds`, `kill`, `waitPid`, `availableParallelism`, `totalMemory`, `setNice`, `setIdlePriority`, `setCpuAffinity`, `monotonicNanos`, `wallClockNanos`, `signalFd`, `readSignal`, `argv`, `platform`, `arch` |
| [`nish:io`](../nish-io.md) | `write`, `writeError`, `writeBytes`, `panic` |
| [`nish:secret`](../nish-secret.md) | `Secret`, `secret`, `expose`, `exposeWith`, `wipe` — the one module with source behind it ([Secrets](#secrets-nishsecret)) |
| [`nish:region`](../nish-region.md) | `Region`, `region`, `regionWith`, `enter`, `enterWith`, `free` — source behind it too ([Regions](#regions-nishregion)) |
| [`nish:net`](../nish-net.md) | `netAddress`, `netLocalPort`, `tcpListen`, `tcpListenFlags`, `tcpAccept`, `netRead`, `netWrite`, `netWrite2`, `netShutdown`, `netClose`, `netMss`, `netSetOption` and its option ids `NET_TCP_NODELAY`, `NET_TCP_QUICKACK`, `NET_SO_KEEPALIVE`, `NET_SO_SNDBUF`, `NET_SO_RCVBUF`, `tcpConnect`, `connectResult`, `udpBind`, `udpSendTo`, `udpRecvFrom`, `pollCreate`, `pollAdd`, `pollModify`, `pollRemove`, `pollWait`, `unixListen`, `unixListenMode`, `unixConnect`, `unixAccept`, `unixSocketPair`, `sendFd`, `recvFd`, `peerCredentials` and the constants `NET_UNIX_UNLINK_STALE`, `NET_UNIX_STREAM`, `NET_UNIX_SEQPACKET` — each a global too ([`nish:net`](#nishnet-addresses-non-blocking-tcp-and-udp-and-the-readiness-loop)) |
| [`nish:term`](../nish-term.md) | `readStdin`, `waitStdin`, `isTerminal`, `terminalSize`, `setRawMode`, `setTerminalRestore` — each a global too ([`nish:term`](#nishterm-terminal-input)) |
| [`nish:unsafe`](../nish-unsafe.md) | `uncheckedGet`, `uncheckedSet`, `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub`, `wrappingMul`, `readCString` — **reached only through the import** ([`nish:unsafe`](#nishunsafe-unchecked-access-and-defined-wrapping)) |
| [`nish:async`](../nish-async.md) | `spawn`, `awaitAll` — **reached only through the import** ([Async functions](declarations.md#async-functions-async-and-await)) |
| [`nish:simd`](../nish-simd.md) | the vector types `u8x16`, `u16x8`, `i32x4`, `u32x4`, `f32x4`, `f64x2` and their constructors, `splatU8x16` … `splatF64x2`, `loadU8x16` … `loadF64x2`, `store`, `extract`, `replace`; the masks `mask8x16` … `mask64x2`; the lane operations `add` … `asF64x2`, among them `shl`, `shr`, `rotl` and `rotr` — **reached only through the import** ([`nish:simd`](#nishsimd-sixteen-byte-vectors), [lane operations](#nishsimd-lane-operations-and-masks)) |

```ts
import { readFileSync } from "nish:fs";
import { argv } from "nish:process";
import { write } from "nish:io";
```

- The forms are the ones every other import allows: a named import, with `as`
  (`tests/cases/io_nish_rename`). Default, namespace, side-effect and type-only
  imports are refused under the same messages a relative specifier gets.
- An unknown module is `` Unknown builtin module `nish:sqlite` ``
  (`reject_nish_unknown_module`); a name a module does not export is
  `` Module `nish:fs` has no export `statSync` ``
  (`reject_nish_unknown_export`). Both list what does exist.
- **An imported builtin cannot be shadowed**, and that is the reason to prefer
  one. A global builtin is consulted only when no user function of that name is
  in scope, so declaring one silently replaces it; declaring one that collides
  with an import is `` `panic` is already declared in this module `` instead
  (`reject_nish_import_clash`).
- A name keeps its kind. `argv`, `platform` and `arch` are values, and calling
  one is refused (`reject_nish_property_call`); the functions are not values,
  for the reason no function in this language is one
  (`reject_nish_builtin_value`).
- `exit` terminates control flow exactly as `process.exit` does, so a
  non-`void` function may end with it (`io_nish_rename`).
- Diagnostics name the canonical builtin whatever the call site calls it:
  `exit(1, 2)` reports `` `process.exit` expects exactly 1 argument ``, which
  is the rule to look up.
- Everything else stays global — `Math.*`, the width conversions,
  `console.log` / `console.error`, `String.fromCharCode`, `Arena.*`, `Ok` and
  `Err`. They lower to an LLVM intrinsic or a single instruction and cost no
  runtime at all, so they read as language rather than as library.
  `String.fromBytes` is global too, beside `String.fromCharCode` on the same
  `String`, though both make their answer with one `nish_str_new`.
  `Date.now()` and `crypto.getRandomValues` are global too, though each is a
  runtime call, because JavaScript spells them as globals and a program that
  runs under Node unchanged has to find them where Node has them
  ([The host](#the-host-the-wall-clock-entropy-file-times-and-signals)).

## `console`

The reference for each of these, with its parameters, its answer and its capability, is its doc comment in [`runtime/nish.d.ts`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/runtime/nish.d.ts); the rules are here.

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `console.log(x: string \| number \| i64 \| f64 \| boolean): void` | Writes `x` and a newline to stdout with one `write(2)`; statement position only; exactly one argument | write | `str_console_log`, `i64_basic`; `reject_console_log_noargs`, `reject_console_log_two_args`, `reject_console_log_as_value`; arrays and objects are rejected (`` `console.log` accepts string, number, or boolean, got i32[] `` *(CLI only)*) |
| `console.error(x): void` | the same, on **stderr** — the stream a compiler's diagnostics belong on (WP14 B2). Identical rules and identical messages under its own name | write | `io_streams`; `reject_console_error_type` |
| `write(s: string): void` | `s` to stdout with **no** trailing newline and no conversion (a `string` only); statement position | write | `io_streams` |
| `writeError(s: string): void` | the same, on stderr | write | `io_streams` |
| `writeBytes(bytes: readonly u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | the bytes of `bytes[off..off+len)` to stdout as they are, answering `len` or a **negative errno** if the stream refuses them, never a panic; a pipe whose reader has gone raises SIGPIPE natively, where Node answers `-32` EPIPE. A range outside `bytes` **panics** with `slice out of range: [off, off+len) of length n` and exits 1 (a `slice` site), under Node too. No capability, as for `write`. A `wasm32` build has no stdout to reach and refuses it | write | `io_write_bytes`, `io_write_bytes_bounds`; `reject_write_bytes_arity`, `reject_write_bytes_type` (NL2268), `reject_write_bytes_wasm` |
| `panic(message: string): void` | `message` and a newline to stderr, then exit 1 — the same ending an out-of-range index has. Statement position, and it **terminates control flow** like `process.exit`, so a non-`void` function may end with it (WP14 D1, WP16) | write | `io_streams`; `reject_panic_value` |

Numbers print as JavaScript's `String(x)`: exact decimal for `i32`/`i64`,
shortest round-trip digits for `f64` (`0.1`, `1e+21`, `1e-7`, `NaN`,
`Infinity`, `-0` as `0`) (`tests/runtime-test.c`, `tests/cases/str_f64_mode`,
`math_intrinsics`). Booleans print `true`/`false`.

Reference: [`nish:io`](../nish-io.md).

## `Math`

The reference for each member of `Math`, with its parameters, its answer and its capability, is its doc comment in [`runtime/nish.d.ts`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/runtime/nish.d.ts); the rules are here.

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Math.sqrt/floor/ceil/trunc/sin/cos/exp/log(x: f64): f64` | LLVM intrinsics (`llvm.sqrt.f64`, ...), except `floor`, `ceil` and `trunc` in an x86-64 module that is not a wasm build: there they call the runtime's `nish_floor`, `nish_ceil` and `nish_trunc`, which run SSE4.1's `roundsd` on a CPU that has it and libm's routine on one that does not, chosen once before `main` (`NISH_SIMD=scalar` pins libm); with no `--target` that is an x86-64 host. The answers are the same bits on either path | none | `math_intrinsics`, `math_rounding`; `reject_math_i32` (`` requires an f64 argument, got i32 (use --number-mode f64 or toF64(x)) ``) |
| `Math.tan(x: f64): f64` | a call to `std/math.ts`'s `tanF64`, fdlibm's, copied into the module as `internal @nish.tanF64`, so no target calls libm; exact near every multiple of π/2 and within one ulp | none | `math_tan`, `math_std_edges` |
| `Math.atan2(y: f64, x: f64): f64`, `Math.hypot(x: f64, y: f64): f64` | calls to `std/math.ts`'s `atan2F64` and `hypotF64`, copied in like `tan`; ECMAScript's special cases (`atan2(0, -0)` is π, `atan2(-0, -0)` is −π, `hypot(Infinity, NaN)` is `Infinity`). `Math.hypot` takes exactly two arguments, not JavaScript's any number | none | `math_atan2`, `math_hypot`; `reject_math_atan2_f32` (`` `Math.atan2` requires an f64 argument, got f32 (use --number-mode f64 or toF64(x)) ``), `reject_math_hypot_arity` (`` `Math.hypot` expects exactly 2 arguments, got 3 ``) |
| `Math.pow(x: f64, y: f64): f64` | `llvm.pow.f64` plus a `select` for the cases where ECMAScript and C99 differ: `pow(x, NaN)` and `pow(±1, ±Infinity)` are `NaN` (C gives `1`); `pow(x, ±0)` is `1`, `pow(NaN, 0)` is `1`, and every other special case agrees with C | none | `math_intrinsics`; `tests/differential/corpus/f64_pow_spec` |
| `Math.round(x: f64): f64` | JavaScript's round-half-up (`Math.floor`'s `floor` + compare + `select`), then `llvm.copysign.f64` puts `x`'s sign back: `2.5` -> `3`, `-2.5` -> `-2`, `0.49999999999999994` -> `0`, and a value in `[-0.5, 0)` or `-0` itself -> `-0`, as in JavaScript; `NaN` -> `NaN` | none | `math_intrinsics`, `math_round_negzero`, `math_rounding` |
| `Math.abs(x: T): T` for any numeric `T` | `llvm.abs.*` (wrapping for `INT_MIN`) / `llvm.fabs.f32` / `llvm.fabs.f64`; on an unsigned type, no instruction at all (the value is its own magnitude) | none | `math_i32`, `math_intrinsics`; `i64`, `f32` and the unsigned widths *(CLI only)* |
| `Math.min(a: T, b: T): T`, `Math.max(a: T, b: T): T` | exactly two operands of one numeric type; signed integers: `llvm.smin/smax`; unsigned: `llvm.umin/umax`; floats: JavaScript's answer, a NaN operand gives NaN and `-0` is below `+0` (`Math.min(0, -0)` is `-0`). A native build branches as clang compiles the C a programmer writes for it: `fcmp uno` to a quiet NaN, else `fcmp olt`/`ogt` and a `select`, and on `fcmp oeq` the operand whose sign bit is set (`min`) or clear (`max`), the three joined by a `phi`; x86 has no instruction for `llvm.minimum`, whose expansion measured 25–55% slower in `bench/math`. A wasm build keeps `llvm.minimum/maximum.<f32\|f64>`, which are wasm's `f64.min`/`f64.max`, so no libm is linked for them | none | `math_i32`, `math_intrinsics`, `math_minmax_float`, `math_minmax_nan`; `reject_math_min_arity` (`` `Math.min` expects exactly 2 arguments, got 1 ``) |
| `Math.clz32(x: i32 \| u32): integer<0, 32>` | the leading zero bits of `x`'s 32 bits, JavaScript's answer (an `i32` and a `u32` are the bits ToUint32 gives): `llvm.ctlz.i32` with `i1 false`, so `0` answers `32`. The answer is ranged (`integer<Lo, Hi>`, see [Types](types.md)), so `31 - Math.clz32(word & (0 - word))`, the index of a word's lowest set bit, needs no overflow check. Any other operand type is refused rather than converted | none | `math_clz32`; `reject_math_clz32_type` (`` `Math.clz32` expects an i32 or a u32, got f64 (convert with toI32 or toU32) ``) |
| `Math.sign(x: T): T` for any numeric `T` | `-1`, `0` or `1` in `x`'s own type (a ranged `x` answers its base type). A float answers `llvm.copysign(1.0, x)` unless `fcmp ueq x, 0.0`, when it answers `x` itself, so `-0` and `NaN` come back as JavaScript gives them; a signed integer is `zext (x > 0) - zext (x < 0)`, an unsigned one `zext (x != 0)` | none | `math_sign`; `reject_math_sign_type` (`` `Math.sign` expects a number, got string ``) |
| `Math.imul(a: i32 \| u32, b: i32 \| u32): i32` | the low 32 bits of the product, read signed: one wrapping `mul i32`, with no overflow check, which is JavaScript's answer for any operands an `i32` or a `u32` holds (`Math.imul(0x7fffffff, 2)` is `-2`). Any other operand type is refused rather than converted, for `Math.clz32`'s reason | none | `math_imul`; `reject_math_imul_f64` (`` `Math.imul` expects an i32 or a u32, got f64 (convert with toI32 or toU32) ``) |
| `Math.random(): f64` | xorshift64\* in the runtime (`nish_random`), 53 random bits in `[0, 1)`, seeded from time and pid | write | `math_random` |
| `Math.PI: f64`, `Math.E: f64` | constants, also in i32 mode | none | `math_i32`, `math_intrinsics` |

The f64-only functions reject `i32`/`i64` arguments; `number` in i32 mode is
an `i32`, so write `Math.sqrt(toF64(n))` or use f64 mode. A numeric literal
argument is typed `f64` by context (`Math.sqrt(2)` works in both modes).

## Numeric conversions

The reference for each conversion, with its parameter and its answer, is its doc comment in [`runtime/nish.d.ts`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/runtime/nish.d.ts); the rules are here.

| Signature | Semantics | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `toI32(x): i32` | narrower or equal width: `trunc` (wraps); wider signed source: `sext`, wider unsigned source: `zext`; a float source (`f32` or `f64`): saturating `llvm.fptosi.sat.i32.<f32\|f64>` (NaN -> 0, out of range clamps); `i32`: identity | `conversions`, `u_conv_roundtrip`; `reject_toi32_string` |
| `toI64(x): i64` | signed source: `sign-extend`; unsigned source: `zext`; `f64`: saturating; `i64`: identity | `conversions`, `u_conv_widths` |
| `toU8`, `toU16`, `toU32`, `toU64` | widening: `zext` from an unsigned source, `sext` from a signed one (so `toU64(-1: i32)` is 2^64 - 1, as `-1i32 as u64` is in Rust); narrowing: `trunc`; a float source: saturating `llvm.fptoui.sat`, whose clamp is `0 .. 2^bits-1`, so a negative value is `0` | `u_conv_widths`, `u_conv_f64`, `u_conv_roundtrip`; `reject_u_conversion_arg` |
| any integer -> an integer of the **same width** and other signedness | **no instruction at all**: signedness is not part of the LLVM type and the bits do not move (`toU32(i)` on an `i32`, `toI64(q)` on a `u64`) | `u_conv_same_width` |
| `toF32(x): f32` | signed integers: `sitofp`; unsigned integers: `uitofp`; `f64`: `fptrunc` (rounds to nearest); `f32`: identity | `f32_conversions`, `f32_constant` |
| `toF64(x): f64` | signed integers: `sitofp`; unsigned integers: `uitofp`; `f32`: `fpext` (exact); `f64`: identity | `conversions`, `u_conv_f64`, `f32_conversions` |
| `f64ToBits(x: f64): i64` | reinterpret the 64 bits, never convert the value: `toI64(1.5)` is `1`, `f64ToBits(1.5)` is `0x3FF8000000000000`. One `bitcast`, so a function that only reinterprets bits stays `readnone` | `conv_f64_bits`; `reject_f64tobits_type`, `reject_f64tobits_arity` |
| `f32ToBits(x: f32): i32` | the same for an `f32`'s 32 bits, signed as an `i32`: `f32ToBits(1.5)` is `0x3FC00000`, and `f32ToBits(-0)` is `-2147483648`. One `bitcast float to i32`; under Node, `runtime/nish.mjs` supplies it from a `DataView` | `f32_to_bits`; `reject_f32_to_bits_f64` (`` `f32ToBits` expects an argument of type f32, got f64 ``) |
| `bitsToF64(b: i64): f64` | the inverse. `bitsToF64(f64ToBits(x)) === x` for every `x` except `NaN`, which is not `===` to itself | `conv_f64_bits`; `reject_bitstof64_type` |
| `Number(x: string \| i32 \| i64 \| f64 \| boolean): f64` | a string is parsed with JavaScript's `Number(s)` rules (below); `i32`/`i64`: `sitofp`; `boolean`: `uitofp` (`true` is `1`); `f64`: identity. A numeric literal argument is typed `f64` (`Number(2.5)` works in i32 mode) | `parse_numbers`; `reject_number_array` (`` `Number` expects a string, number, or boolean, got i32[] ``) |
| `parseInt(s: string): i32` | base 10 only: ASCII whitespace, an optional sign, then digits (`strtoll`); stops at the first other character. **Deviations from JavaScript:** no `NaN` in an `i32`, so no digits give `0` (`parseInt("abc")`, `parseInt("")`); values beyond the `i32` range saturate exactly like `toI32` (`parseInt("99999999999")` is `2147483647`); a `0x` prefix is not hexadecimal (`parseInt("0x10")` is `0`). Always `i32`, also under `--number-mode f64` (use `Number` there) | `parse_numbers`; `reject_parseint_number` (`` `parseInt` expects a string, got i32 ``) |
| `parseFloat(s: string): f64` | ASCII whitespace, then the longest decimal literal (`[sign] digits [. digits] [e [sign] digits]`, `. digits`, or `[sign] Infinity`), correctly rounded by `strtod`; `NaN` when there is none (`parseFloat("abc")`, `""`, `"."`); `parseFloat("3.14xyz")` is `3.14`, `"1e"` is `1`. **Deviation:** a `0x` prefix is read as hexadecimal like `strtod` (`parseFloat("0x1A")` is `26`; JavaScript stops at the `x` and gives `0`) | `parse_numbers` |

The string parsers accept only ASCII whitespace (` \t\n\v\f\r`), not the
Unicode spaces JavaScript also trims. `Number(s)` trims it on both sides and
then requires the whole string to be one literal: `Number("")` and
`Number("   ")` are `0`, `Number("  7.5  ")` is `7.5`, `Number("12px")`,
`Number("1e")`, `Number("Infinityx")`, `Number("nan")` and `Number("inf")`
are `NaN`, `Number("0x1A")` is `26` (as in JavaScript; hex floats such as
`0x1p3` are also accepted by `strtod`, which JavaScript rejects), and the
`0b`/`0o` prefixes are `NaN` (JavaScript reads them). All three lower to
`nish_parse_number(s, mode)` in the runtime (mode 0 `parseFloat`, 1 `Number`,
2 `parseInt`, the last followed by `llvm.fptosi.sat.i32.f64`); their effect
is write (`strtod`/`strtoll` may set `errno`), so a function that parses is
never `readonly` ([wp7-runtime.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp7-runtime.md#string-to-number)).

## `nish:unsafe`: unchecked access and defined wrapping

Two things the language otherwise never does are each a decision about one
site: reading or writing an element without the bounds check, and letting a
signed `+ - *` wrap. `nish:unsafe` holds the five functions that make them,
and a sixth, `readCString`, that reads a C string through a pointer nothing
proves. A program reaches them only through an import, so every module that
gives up a check or defines a wrap says so at its top and every site that does
is a call a reader can find.

Reference: [`nish:unsafe`](../nish-unsafe.md).

| Signature | Lowering | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `uncheckedGet(xs: T[], i: i32): T` | the GEP and load `xs[i]` lowers to, with no `len` load, no compare and no branch to the bounds panic | read | `unsafe_get_set`; `reject_unsafe_arity`, `reject_unsafe_type` |
| `uncheckedSet(xs: T[], i: i32, v: T): void` | the GEP and store `xs[i] = v` lowers to, likewise unchecked; a statement | write | `unsafe_get_set`; `reject_unsafe_arity`, `reject_unsafe_type`, `reject_unsafe_par_shared_write` |
| `wrappingAdd(a: T, b: T): T` | `add`, never `nsw` and never checked | none | `unsafe_wrapping`; `reject_unsafe_arity`, `reject_unsafe_type` |
| `wrappingSub(a: T, b: T): T` | `sub`, never `nsw` and never checked | none | `unsafe_wrapping`; `reject_unsafe_type` |
| `wrappingMul(a: T, b: T): T` | `mul`, never `nsw` and never checked | none | `unsafe_wrapping`; `reject_unsafe_type` |
| `readCString(p: CPtr): string` | a call to `@nish.ffi.str`, the scan-and-copy a `string` result of a `declare function` uses ([`readCString`](declarations.md#readcstring-a-string-out-of-a-buffer-c-owns)) | read; allocates | `ffi_owned_string`; `reject_unsafe_read_cstring`, `reject_ffi_owned_string_arena` |

- **The import is required.** The six are declared as globals in
  `runtime/nish.d.ts`, as every `nish:` export is, so `tsc` reads either
  spelling; the compiler refuses the global one with
  `` `uncheckedGet` is a `nish:unsafe` function and is called only through an import of it ``
  (NL2456, `reject_unsafe_no_import`). An import may rename (`as`) and cannot
  be shadowed, as every builtin import (above). A user function of the same
  name, with no import, is the user's function, as with every builtin.
- **`uncheckedGet` and `uncheckedSet` take an array of numbers**: `i32`,
  `i64`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32` or `f64` elements, and nothing else
  is `` `uncheckedGet` takes an array of numbers (i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, f32 or f64), got string[] ``
  (NL2455). A number is copied in and out and held by nothing, so the store
  needs none of the escape and inline-array reasoning `xs[i] = v` carries. The
  index is an `i32`, and an `f64` one is
  `` `uncheckedGet` expects an argument of type i32, got f64 ``; the value of a
  store is the element type. A `readonly` array may be read and not written
  (`` Cannot `uncheckedSet` through readonly u8[] ``). An index outside
  `[0, xs.length)` is undefined behaviour, which is the whole of the trade.
  The receiver is an argument, so an array field handed to either is a value
  and is not stored inline ([Fixed-length array fields are stored
  inline](expressions.md#fixed-length-array-fields-are-stored-inline)); a store is a write
  of the receiver for every rule that asks, the parallel-body rule included
  (`reject_unsafe_par_shared_write`).
- **`wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub` and `wrappingMul` take two operands of one
  type, `i32` or `i64`**, which is also the answer: the signed words are the
  ones whose operators are checked, and an unsigned operator already wraps.
  `` `wrappingMul` takes i32 or i64 operands (convert with toI32 or toI64), got u32 ``
  is NL2454, and two widths are
  `` `wrappingAdd` needs every operand of one type, got i32 and i64 `` (NL2400,
  as `ctSelect`'s). A bare literal takes the other operand's type, wherever it
  stands. The answer is the two's-complement wrap at that width, defined for
  every pair (`unsafe_wrapping`). In a module
  constant's initialiser the call folds, wrapping, where `2147483647 + 1` is
  refused ([Module constants](declarations.md#module-constants)).
- **Under Node** `runtime/nish.mjs` answers the import; a program that stays
  in range prints the same as natively (`unsafe_get_set` and
  `unsafe_wrapping` are run both ways by `tests/run.js`). `readCString` has no
  Node form: its `CPtr` comes only from a `declare function`, which Node cannot
  call, so a program that reads one is native only, as every FFI program is
  outside the differential oracle (`docs/wp27-ffi.md` §5).
- **Every import and every call is a recorded fact.** `--emit-checked` prints,
  per module, an `unsafe import <line>:<col> <name> from "nish:unsafe"` line for
  each name imported and an `unsafe call <line>:<col> <name> (node <id>)` line
  for each site, so a report of where a program opts out of a check reads them
  rather than the source (`tests/self/goldens/checked/`, one file per module).
- **The import is the opt-in the no-panic scope takes.** Under `--deny-panics`
  or `"nish".noPanic`, `uncheckedGet` and `uncheckedSet` are allowed, listed
  as `unchecked` sites with `"allowed": true`, because they cannot panic and
  the import has already said, at the top of the module, that an index out of
  range is the author's to rule out ([The no-panic scope](semantics-decisions.md#the-no-panic-scope),
  `deny_panics_unsafe`). `readCString` is an allowed `unchecked` site on the
  same terms, with its copy's `oom` beside it (`ffi_owned_string`). The
  `wrapping*` three are not sites at all: they are defined for every pair.
- **To the bounds proof `uncheckedGet` and `uncheckedSet` are the load and
  the store** `xs[i]` and `xs[i] = v` are, less the check: a call moves no
  length, so in `uncheckedGet(a, at[0]) + b[at[1]]` with `at` an array of
  two, `at[1]` stays proven after the call. Neither records a passed check,
  because neither has one: a checked `xs[i]` after either keeps its check,
  and a resize in the value stored still takes the length away
  (`tests/cases/arr_bounds_unchecked_kept`).
- **There is no flag that turns the checks off.** `--unchecked-indexing` and
  `--wrapping` were removed before 1.0, and the CLI refuses each with exit 2
  and a line naming its replacement (`` `--wrapping` is gone ``,
  `tests/nish/cli.ts`): an opt-out is written at the site, where `--emit-checked`
  and the no-panic scope can see it.

## `nish:simd`: sixteen-byte vectors

A vector is sixteen bytes of lanes of one number type, held and passed as one
value: an LLVM `<N x T>` in a register, a local, a field or an array slot. The
module names six of them, and the calls that make one, read one out of an
array, write one back and take one lane out or put one in. Nothing here names a
target: the IR is `insertelement`, `shufflevector`, `extractelement` and a
vector `load` or `store`, and LLVM picks the instructions (`tests/run.js`'s
`simd` section greps every `simd_*.ll` for `llvm.x86.` and `llvm.aarch64.`).
The lane operations, the masks a compare answers and the shifts are in
[the next section](#nishsimd-lane-operations-and-masks).

The six are `u8x16` (`<16 x i8>`), `u16x8` (`<8 x i16>`), `i32x4` and `u32x4`
(`<4 x i32>`), `f32x4` (`<4 x float>`) and `f64x2` (`<2 x double>`). Each has
a constructor of one argument per lane, a splat (`splatU8x16` … `splatF64x2`)
and a load (`loadU8x16` … `loadF64x2`) from an array of its lane type; the
table below spells each family with `i32x4`.

Reference: [`nish:simd`](../nish-simd.md).

| Signature | Lowering | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `i32x4(a, b, c, d)`, one argument per lane | one `insertelement` per lane into `undef`, which `opt` folds to a constant vector when every lane is one | `simd_lanes`; `reject_simd_arity`, `reject_simd_lane_type` |
| `splatI32x4(x)` | one `insertelement` into lane 0 and a `shufflevector` whose mask is `zeroinitializer` | `simd_lanes` |
| `loadI32x4(xs, i)` | one bounds check for the whole vector, `i < len` and `i + N <= len`, branching to `nish_panic_index(i, len)`; then the element's address bitcast to `<N x T>*` and one `load` aligned to the lane | `simd_access`, `simd_access_oob`, `simd_access_oob_first`, `simd_access_oob_negative`; `reject_simd_lane_type` |
| `store(v, xs, i)` | the same check, then one `store`; a statement | `simd_access`, `simd_store_oob`; `reject_simd_lane_type`, `reject_simd_arity` |
| `extract(v, k)` | `extractelement` at the constant `k` | `simd_lanes`; `reject_simd_lane_index` |
| `replace(v, k, x)` | `insertelement` at the constant `k`: a new vector, `v` unchanged | `simd_lanes`, `simd_values`; `reject_simd_lane_index` |

- **The import is required.** The six types and every call are declared in
  `runtime/nish.d.ts` under `declare module "nish:simd"` only, and a module
  that spells one without the import is refused with
  `` `i32x4` is a `nish:simd` name and is used only through an import of it: add `import { i32x4 } from "nish:simd"` ``
  (NL2578, `reject_simd_no_import`). An import may rename (`as`) and cannot be
  shadowed, as every builtin import.
- **A load or store takes an array of the lane type, exactly**: a `u8x16` is
  loaded from a `u8[]` and nothing else, so the sixteen bytes it reads are the
  sixteen elements the index names, and an `f64[]` handed to `loadF32x4` is
  `` `loadF32x4` takes an array whose elements are the vector's lane type, f32[], got f64[] ``
  (NL2579). A `readonly` array may be loaded from and not stored to
  (`` Cannot `store` through readonly u8[] ``). The index is an `i32`; the
  check is one compare pair for the whole vector, so a load whose last lane is
  past the end panics before it reads, naming a lane past the end (the first
  when it is out of range, else the last) and the length, as `xs[i]` does (`simd_access_oob`, run by `tests/run.js` natively and under
  Node). The access is aligned to the lane, not to sixteen: an array's
  elements are where the arena put them.
- **A lane index is an integer literal in range.** `extract(v, k)` and
  `replace(v, k, x)` take `k` as a literal from 0 to one less than the lane
  count, because a constant lane is one instruction and needs no check at run
  time: a variable is
  `` `extract` takes a lane index that is an integer literal, from 0 to 3: i32x4 has 4 lanes `` (NL2580)
  and a literal past the end is
  `` `extract` lane index 4 is out of range for i32x4, whose lanes are 0 to 3 `` (NL2583,
  `reject_simd_lane_index`). The first argument must be a vector
  (`` `extract` takes a `nish:simd` vector as its first argument, got i32 ``, NL2582),
  and a lane given to a constructor, a splat or `replace` is the lane type, as
  any argument is (`reject_simd_lane_type`).
- **A vector is a value.** It is copied by assignment, passed and returned in
  registers, and held in a local, a class field or an array (`simd_values`).
  In an object or an array it is sixteen bytes aligned to sixteen, the layout
  clang gives `__attribute__((vector_size(16)))`, which `tests/layout/simd.c`
  asserts against the IR's struct and reads lane by lane; an array of vectors
  steps by sixteen. The arena hands out objects aligned to eight, so a field
  access is `align 8`.
- **A vector has no operators, and no comparison.** `+`, unary `-`, a
  truthiness test, a template hole and `console.log` of a whole vector or a
  mask are refused with the usual operand-type diagnostics
  (`reject_simd_operators`); the lane-wise forms are the functions of the next
  section. `===`, `!==`, `<` and the rest, and the `===` inside an array's
  `indexOf`, are
  `` `===` does not compare `nish:simd` vectors or masks (got i32x4): compare lane by lane with `eq`, `lt` and the rest, which answer a mask, and ask it `all` or `any` ``
  (NL2581, `reject_simd_compare`): a lane-wise compare answers a mask, not a
  boolean, and under Node a vector is a typed array whose `===` is identity. A
  vector is not a `Map` key (`reject_simd_map_key`), not `Secret`
  (`reject_simd_secret`) and not nullable (`reject_simd_nullable`).
- **Under Node** `runtime/nish.mjs` resolves the import to `runtime/core.mjs`,
  where a vector is a typed array whose element type does the lane's
  arithmetic. `--emit-ts` writes the import as `nish/runtime`'s. A load or a
  store checks the whole vector and panics with the native words.
  `tests/run.js`'s `simd` section runs every `simd_*` program with a `.out`
  natively, under `--profile wasi` (where a sysroot is installed) and under
  Node, and holds the three to one output.
- **A vector does not cross the interop boundary yet.** An exported function
  whose parameter or result holds a vector at any depth (the vector itself,
  an array of them, a `Result` with a vector arm, an array of a class that
  holds one) is left out of `--emit-header`, `--emit-napi` and the
  `--emit-dts` typings and wasm loader, with a comment naming the type, as
  every type the sidecars cannot spell is. A class that holds a vector
  anywhere (a field, an element, a `Result` arm, another class it points at)
  is opaque in the header (`typedef struct Name Name;`), as a `Map` or
  `Secret` holder is: C has no portable vector type to lay it out with. A bare
  pointer to such a class still crosses, as an opaque `struct Name *`.

## `nish:simd`: lane operations and masks

Every operation on a vector is a free function of `nish:simd`, because a
TypeScript program cannot overload `+`. The operand types pick the lowering,
and each lowers to LLVM vector IR or a target-independent `llvm.*` intrinsic:
no golden holds `llvm.x86.` or `llvm.aarch64.` ([wp38-simd.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp38-simd.md)
§3.2).

Reference: [`nish:simd`](../nish-simd.md).

| Signature | Lowering | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div(a, b)` on `f32x4`, `f64x2` | `fadd`, `fsub`, `fmul`, `fdiv`, no fast-math flags | `simd_ops_float`; `reject_simd_op_operands` |
| `neg`, `abs`, `sqrt(a)` on `f32x4`, `f64x2` | `fneg`, `llvm.fabs`, `llvm.sqrt` | `simd_ops_float`; `reject_simd_op_operands` |
| `addWrapping`, `subWrapping`, `mulWrapping(a, b)` on `u8x16`, `u16x8`, `i32x4`, `u32x4` | `add`, `sub`, `mul` with no `nsw` or `nuw`: each lane wraps | `simd_ops_int`; `reject_simd_op_operands` |
| `shl(v, n)`, `shr(v, n)`, `n` a literal below the lane width | `shl`; `shr` is `lshr` on an unsigned lane and `ashr` on `i32x4` | `simd_shifts`; `reject_simd_shift_count` |
| `rotl(v, n)`, `rotr(v, n)` on the same four | `llvm.fshl`, `llvm.fshr` with `v` as both halves | `simd_shifts`, `simd_chacha_quarter`; `reject_simd_shift_count` |
| `and`, `or`, `xor(a, b)`, `not(a)` on an integer vector or a mask | `and`, `or`, `xor`; `not` is `xor` with all-ones | `simd_ops_int` |
| `min`, `max(a, b)` on every vector | `llvm.umin`/`smin`/`umax`/`smax`; floats `llvm.minimum`/`llvm.maximum`, NaN-propagating with -0 below +0, as `Math.min` | `simd_ops_int`, `simd_ops_float` |
| `eq`, `ne`, `lt`, `le`, `gt`, `ge(a, b)` | `icmp` (unsigned on `u*` lanes) or ordered `fcmp` (`une` for `ne`), answering the lane width's mask | `simd_ops_int`, `simd_ops_float`; `reject_simd_op_operands` |
| `select(m, a, b)` | `select`: lane `k` of `a` where lane `k` of `m` is set, else of `b` | `simd_ops_int`; `reject_simd_op_operands` |
| `any(m)`, `all(m)` | `llvm.vector.reduce.or`, `.and` on `<N x i1>` | `simd_ops_int` |
| `bitmask(m)`, an `i32` with bit `k` lane `k` | `bitcast <N x i1>` to `iN`, `zext` | `simd_ops_int` |
| `sum(v)` on `u8x16`, `u16x8` (an `i32`, exact) and `f32x4`, `f64x2` (the lane type, lanes added 0 to N-1) | `zext` and `llvm.vector.reduce.add`; floats `llvm.vector.reduce.fadd` without `reassoc` | `simd_ops_int`, `simd_ops_float`; `reject_simd_sum` |
| `sumWrapping(v)` on `i32x4` (an `i32`) and `u32x4` (a `u32`) | `llvm.vector.reduce.add`, wrapping | `simd_ops_int`; `reject_simd_sum` |
| `shuffle(a, b, i0, …)`, one literal index per lane, from 0 to 2N-1 | `shufflevector` | `simd_ops_int`; `reject_simd_shuffle` |
| `asU8x16(v)` … `asF64x2(v)` | `bitcast`: the same sixteen bytes read as other lanes | `simd_ops_int` |

- **Every operand is one vector type.** Two types are
  `` `min` takes operands of one type, got i32x4 and u32x4; reinterpret the lanes with `asU8x16` and the rest ``,
  a scalar where a vector goes is
  `` `eq` takes a `nish:simd` vector, got i32 `` (NL2638), and a vector a
  family does not take names the family:
  `` `add` is float lane arithmetic and takes an `f32x4` or an `f64x2`, got i32x4: an integer lane can overflow, so its form is `addWrapping` ``
  (NL2623, `reject_simd_op_operands`). Integer lane arithmetic wraps, and its
  name says so: making a lane trap as scalar `+` does would cost the speed the
  type is for.
- **A shift count is a literal below the lane width.** `shl`, `shr`, `rotl`
  and `rotr` take the count as an integer literal from 0 to 7, 15 or 31, so
  each is one instruction with a splat constant and nothing is shifted by a
  variable: a variable count is
  `` `shl` takes a count that is an integer literal below the lane width, from 0 to 31: a lane of u32x4 is 32 bits `` (NL2630),
  and the width or more is
  `` `rotl` count 32 is not below the lane width of u32x4, 32 bits: a shift by the width or more moves every bit out, and a rotate by it is a rotate by 0 ``
  (NL2631, `reject_simd_shift_count`). LLVM gives a shift by the width no
  meaning, and a rotate by it is a rotate by 0. They are what ChaCha20,
  SHA-256 and other add-rotate-xor code is built from (`simd_chacha_quarter`).
- **A mask is a compare's answer, held only as a value.** `eq` and the rest on
  two vectors answer `mask8x16`, `mask16x8`, `mask32x4` or `mask64x2` by lane
  width, an `<N x i1>`; there is no constructor
  (`` `mask32x4` is a mask type and has no constructor: a mask is what a lane-wise compare (`eq`, `lt` and the rest) answers ``,
  NL2621). `select` takes the mask of its vectors' width
  (`` `select` between two i32x4 takes the mask their compare answers, mask32x4, got mask64x2 ``,
  NL2629). A mask lives in a local, a parameter or the return of a function
  the module keeps, and is
  `` `mask32x4` cannot be a field: a `nish:simd` mask is a value held only in a local, a parameter or a return of a function this module keeps; store the vectors it selects, or its `bitmask` ``
  (NL2622) as a field, an array element, a `Result` arm, a type argument, a
  method's parameter or result, or an exported signature
  (`reject_simd_mask_storage`, `reject_simd_mask_in_body`): it has no size in
  memory that all three targets share.
- **A sum says whether it wraps.** `sum` of `u8x16` or `u16x8` adds in an
  `i32` and cannot overflow; `sum` of `i32x4` or `u32x4` can, and is
  `` `sum` of i32x4 can overflow its lane type, so its total is `sumWrapping`, which wraps as the lanes do ``
  (NL2636, `reject_simd_sum`). A float sum adds lane 0 first and lane N-1
  last, so it is the same bits on every target.
- **A shuffle names every lane.** `shuffle(a, b, …)` takes one literal per
  lane of the answer, each from 0 to 2N-1, where N and up are `b`'s lanes;
  a wrong count, a variable or an index past the end is refused
  (NL2632 to NL2635, `reject_simd_shuffle`).
- **Under Node** each operation is a function of `runtime/core.mjs` over the
  typed arrays, and a mask is an array of booleans. `tests/run.js`'s `simd`
  section holds the native, WASI and Node outputs to one.

## Constant time: `ctSelect` and `ctEq`

Crypto code must not branch on a secret or index memory by one, and LLVM
promises neither: a `select` it can see through may become a branch, and a mask
it can prove is a boolean may become a `select`. These two builtins are how a
program selects and compares on a secret without giving the optimiser that
choice (WP34 N6).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ctSelect(mask: T, a: T, b: T): T` | `(a & mask) \| (b & ~mask)`: `a` when `mask` is all-ones, `b` when it is zero | none | `ct_select_u32`, `ct_u64`; `reject_ct_select_i32`, `reject_ct_select_i32_literal`, `reject_ct_select_f64`, `reject_ct_select_f32`, `reject_ct_select_bool_mask`, `reject_ct_select_mixed`, `reject_ct_select_arity`, `reject_ct_select_float_mask` |
| `ctEq(a: T, b: T): T` | all-ones of `T` when `a === b`, zero otherwise | none | `ct_eq_u32`, `ct_u64`; `reject_ct_eq_i64`, `reject_ct_eq_u8`, `reject_ct_eq_f64`, `reject_ct_eq_f32`, `reject_ct_eq_bool`, `reject_ct_eq_ranged`, `reject_ct_eq_mixed`, `reject_ct_eq_arity`, `reject_ct_eq_literals`, `reject_ct_eq_value` |

- **`T` is `u32` or `u64`, one type for every operand.** A mask is a bit
  pattern, and the unsigned words are the only types whose all-ones is not also
  a number with a sign: `i32`, `i64`, the narrow `u8` and `u16`, a ranged
  integer (an `i32` underneath, and named so), `f32`, `f64` and `boolean` are
  each `` `ctEq` takes u32 or u64 operands (convert with toU32 or toU64), got i64 ``
  (NL2399). A boolean in particular is not a mask: `ctEq` makes the mask
  without the compare a boolean would need. Operands of two types are
  `` `ctSelect` needs every operand of one type, got u32 and u64 `` (NL2400),
  since a `u32` mask over `u64` words would leave half of each unselected. The
  type is judged at the operand it was read from before any other operand is
  measured against it, so a boolean mask is told the first message rather than
  the second, and `ctSelect(m, 0x80000000, 0)` on an `i32` mask is NL2399
  rather than "does not fit in i32" (`reject_ct_select_i32_literal`).
- **A bare numeric literal takes its type from the first operand that is not
  one**, wherever it stands: `ctEq(0, x)` and `ctSelect(m, a, 0)` are both
  words of `x`'s and `m`'s type. A fraction is then refused as a fraction
  (`` Non-integer literal `0.5` where u32 is expected ``,
  `reject_ct_select_float_mask`), and with nothing but literals there is no
  width to take, so `ctEq(1, 2)` is an `i32` and refused (`reject_ct_eq_literals`).
- **The mask convention is all-ones or zero, and it is not checked**, because
  the check would be the branch. `ctEq` only ever answers one of the two. Any
  other mask is a defined bitwise blend, bit by bit as the formula says —
  `ctSelect(0xf0f0f0f0, a, b)` takes the high nibble of each byte from `a` —
  and the Node reading below computes the same blend (`ct_select_u32`).
- **They are globals, not a `nish:` module**, by the rule
  [Builtin modules](#builtin-modules-nish) sets: what is backed by the C runtime
  may be imported, and what lowers to instructions reads as language. These call
  nothing (`reject_ct_nish_module`). Like every function, neither is a value
  (`reject_ct_eq_value`).
- **The lowering is the formula behind an optimisation barrier.** The barrier is
  an empty inline `asm` that hands a value back in the same register —
  `call i32 asm "", "=r,0"(i32 %mask) readnone nounwind` — which costs no
  instruction and which no pass can see into, the idiom BoringSSL and Rust's
  `subtle` crate use. `ctSelect` puts it on the mask before the blend; `ctEq`
  computes `((d | -d) >>> (w - 1)) - 1` from `d = a ^ b` and puts it on the
  answer, so a caller's `ctSelect(ctEq(a, b), x, y)` never shows LLVM a
  boolean. `readnone nounwind` is what clang writes on the same statement and is
  true of an empty string, so a function that only selects stays `readnone`.
  [IR_COOKBOOK.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#ctselect-and-cteq) shows the IR. Without the
  barrier `opt -O2` folds `ctSelect(ctEq(a, b), x, y)` into one `select` on
  `a === b` — `tests/run.js` checks both halves of that sentence, so it learns
  if LLVM ever sees through the `asm` or stops needing it.
- **What the barrier promises: no branch and no secret-indexed load in these
  primitives**, checked where the promise lives, in the machine code.
  `tests/run.js` compiles every `tests/cases/ct_asm_*` fixture with
  `clang -O2 -S` for x86-64 and aarch64 and reads each function a fixture names
  by its symbol (`tests/ct-asm.js`). It refuses any conditional branch
  (`j<cc>`, `b.<cond>`, `cbz`, `tbz` and the rest), any call or jump out of
  the function, and any load or store whose address a secret reaches,
  following secrets through registers, flags and stack slots and erring
  towards refusal wherever its model of the machine is not exact. The fixtures are both builtins at both widths, a mask
  straight into a select, a 32-byte MAC compare over `u8[]` and a table read
  that loads every entry (`ct_asm_primitives`, `ct_asm_mac`); and
  `ct_asm_refused` holds an early-exit compare and a secret-indexed table
  lookup that the check must refuse, one for each kind, so a check that read
  nothing fails.
- **It also refuses an instruction whose latency follows a secret**: an
  integer divide (`div`/`idiv`, `udiv`/`sdiv`) or a floating divide or square
  root whose operand a secret reaches (the `latency` kind, seeded by
  `ct_asm_refused`'s `secretDivide`). It reads what `clang -O2` emits for the
  baseline CPU of each target, and for x86-64 at `x86-64-v3`, the one level
  [`--cpu`](semantics-decisions.md#the-cpu-level) offers, and nothing else, so a build with another
  profile or `-march` is not what was read
  ([docs/security/ct-verification.md](../../security/ct-verification.md), CT-2, CT-16).
  It reads only the functions a fixture names, so a module function that is
  not one — every loop in `std/crypto`, for instance — rests on review; that
  record lists them.
- **What it does not promise: anything about the caller's own code.**
  `if (ctEq(a, b) !== 0)` branches on a secret because the program wrote a
  branch; `table[secret]` indexes by one; `===` on a secret is a compare LLVM
  may branch on; a loop whose trip count is secret leaks it; and `/` and `%`
  take time that depends on their operands on many processors. The fixtures
  show the shapes that stay constant time, and a new one belongs beside them.
  On `wasm32` the builtins compile with the same barrier, but the engine
  compiles the module again, so the `.s` this check could read is not what
  runs and nothing is promised there. Weekly, and never from `npm test`,
  `.github/workflows/ct-timing.yml` runs `tests/ct-timing.js` on an x86-64 and
  an aarch64 runner — a dudect-style Welch's t-test of every function the
  fixtures name, a fixed secret against a random one, filed as an issue when
  |t| passes 4.5 — which measures whether their running time on that hardware
  moves with the secret, and cannot promise more: a difference below a shared
  runner's noise, a secret index into a table that fits in the L1 cache, or
  another processor goes unseen.

The TypeScript reading ([wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §2):
`runtime/nish.mjs` supplies both as pure functions of their operands, so the
answers agree and only the timing is not claimed. Over **`u32`** they are
**class A**: a `u32` is a `number` there, the shim puts each answer back in
range with `>>> 0` (JavaScript's `&` answers a signed 32-bit integer), and
`ct_select_u32` and `ct_eq_u32` run unmodified under the prelude and print what
the native build prints. Over **`u64`** the prelude takes BigInts and answers
BigInts, and the `ct_prelude` check in `tests/run.js` holds its answers to
`ct_u64`'s native output line for line. A `u64` program is still **class C**
under Node, as all 64-bit arithmetic is ([RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md)):
a bare `u64` literal is a `number` there, and mixing one with a BigInt throws a
`TypeError` rather than comparing the two and answering zero.

## Wiping a secret: `secureZero`

A key, a secret scalar or another secret intermediate has to be cleared once it
is used, and a store the program never reads again is exactly what the optimiser
removes: `key.fill(0)` just before a key goes out of scope is a dead store at
`-O2`, and a `memset` in the runtime is one too once `-flto` inlines it into
that caller. This builtin is the store that stays (#385).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `secureZero(bytes: u8[]): void` | every byte of `bytes` set to zero, in stores no optimisation removes; an empty array is a call that clears nothing; a statement | write | `wipe_bytes`; `reject_wipe_i32`, `reject_wipe_string`, `reject_wipe_readonly`, `reject_wipe_value`, `reject_wipe_arity`, `reject_wipe_region` |

- **A `u8[]` only**, as `crypto.getRandomValues` takes, because the byte is the
  unit a secret is written in: anything else is
  `` `secureZero` fills a `u8[]`, got i32[] `` (NL2402), a string included,
  which is immutable and has nothing to clear (`reject_wipe_i32`,
  `reject_wipe_string`). The call writes its argument, so a `readonly u8[]` is
  `` Cannot `secureZero` through readonly u8[] (declare it u8[] to write through it) ``
  (NL2264, `reject_wipe_readonly`), and a function that wipes a parameter does
  not get `readonly` on it (`wipe_bytes`). In a scope's region it is refused
  where `fill` is (NL2394, `reject_wipe_region`).
- **A statement**: there is nothing to answer, so
  `` `secureZero` returns void and can only be used as a statement `` (NL2105,
  `reject_wipe_value`), and it takes exactly one argument (NL2061,
  `reject_wipe_arity`).
- **The lowering is one call**, `call void @nish_wipe(%struct.nish_array* %key)`,
  declared `nounwind willreturn` and `nocapture` without `readonly` and with no
  memory attribute, so LLVM may not treat it as a store it can drop.
  `nish_wipe` in `runtime/runtime.c` writes each byte through a `volatile`
  pointer, which the C standard makes behaviour no optimisation may remove
  even once LTO has inlined the body, and is `noinline` besides, so the call
  stays visible in a disassembly. [IR_COOKBOOK.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#securezero)
  shows the IR.
- **It is pinned under `-O2 -flto`, where it matters.** The runtime unit test
  builds a probe the way `--link` builds, `-O2 -flto` over the runtime's
  sources: a key written to a block, used, wiped and freed, then read back
  through a pointer the optimiser cannot follow. With no wipe the key is still
  there, and with a `memset` wipe in another translation unit it is still there
  too, dropped as a store before `free`; with `nish_wipe` nothing is left. The
  same test fails when `nish_wipe` is written as a `memset`.
- **What it does not promise: the copies the program made.** It clears the
  bytes of the array it is handed. A copy taken before (`slice`, a `push` into
  another array, an element read into a local, a register spilled to the stack)
  is the program's to clear, and nothing clears what the operating system
  swapped out.
- **It is a global, and not in a `nish:` module.** It is backed by the C
  runtime, so by the rule [Builtin modules](#builtin-modules-nish) sets it may
  be imported, but no module exports it yet. It works under the wasi profile,
  which links `runtime.c`; a freestanding wasm module has no `nish_wipe`:
  it links `runtime-wasm.c`, which supplies the arena, arrays, the panics and
  `floor`/`ceil`/`trunc` but no wipe, and, when it uses
  strings, `runtime-text.c`, which has the strings and the digits but not the
  wipe.

The TypeScript reading ([wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §2) is
**class A**: `runtime/nish.mjs` supplies it as a loop that sets every element
to zero, and `wipe_bytes` prints the same lines under the prelude as natively.
What Node cannot promise is the native build's stronger claim, because a
collector that moved the array may have left the old bytes behind.

## Who owns a path: `lstatOwnerModeSync`, `geteuid` and `isExecutableSync`

What a driver asks before it trusts a directory or a program it found on its
own: who owns this path, may anyone else write to it, and will the shell run
it (#386; [security/cli.md](../../security/cli.md), CLI-7 and CLI-9).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lstatOwnerModeSync(path: string): i64` | one `lstat` of `path`: the owner's uid in the high 32 bits and `st_mode` (the file type and the permission bits) in the low 32, or **-1** when the path does not resolve or holds a NUL. A symbolic link answers for **itself**, not for what it names | write | `owner_checks`; `reject_owner_arity`, `reject_owner_i32`, `reject_owner_wasm` |
| `geteuid(): i64` | the effective user id, the one to compare an owner with | write | `owner_checks`; `reject_owner_euid_arity`, `reject_owner_euid_wasm` |
| `isExecutableSync(path: string): boolean` | `access(path, X_OK)`: whether the real user may run `path`. `false` for a path that does not resolve or holds a NUL | write | `owner_checks`; `reject_owner_type`, `reject_owner_exec_wasm` |

- **The owner and the mode are one answer.** Both come out of one `lstat`, so
  they describe the same file however the path changes in between; two calls
  could describe two. Take them apart with `(om >> 32) & 0xffffffff` (the
  owner) and `om & 0xfff` (the permission bits) or `om & 0xf000` (the type:
  `0x8000` a regular file, `0x4000` a directory, `0xa000` a symbolic link).
  The mask is not optional: a uid is unsigned and one of 2^31 or more fills
  bit 63, which `>>` on an `i64` copies down, so `om >> 32` alone answers a
  negative owner for a file such a user owns and never equals their
  `geteuid()`. `>>>` would say the same natively, but a BigInt has no `>>>`, so
  the mask is the spelling that reads the same under Node (`owner_checks`). A uid fills
  32 bits, so the answer is an `i64` in both number modes, as `geteuid`'s is,
  and an `i32` is refused rather than truncated
  (`` Cannot initialize i32 variable `om` with i64 ``, `reject_owner_i32`).
- **Not following a link is the point.** A directory that is a symbolic link
  to one this user owns is not a directory this user owns, and the test of a
  path that has to be trusted is of the path as written. That a link answers
  for itself is pinned by RT-9 in `tests/runtime-test.c`, since a program
  cannot make one.
- **`isExecutableSync` is the shell's question,** asked for the real user as
  `access` asks it: a file with no execute bit is not executable, root
  included, and a readable file is not the same answer.
- **Refused on a wasm32 build,** as `statMtimeSync` is: there is no file system
  and no user there, so each is
  `` `lstatOwnerModeSync` reaches the operating system, and a wasm32 build has none to reach ``
  (`reject_owner_wasm`, `reject_owner_euid_wasm`, `reject_owner_exec_wasm`).
  Each takes exactly its arguments (NL2061, `reject_owner_arity`,
  `reject_owner_euid_arity`), and a path is a `string`
  (`reject_owner_type`).
- **The lowering is one call each,** `call i64 @nish_lstat_owner_mode(i8* %p)`,
  `call i64 @nish_euid()` and `call zeroext i1 @nish_is_executable(i8* %p)`,
  declared `nounwind willreturn` and ordered with every write, because the file
  system is not memory LLVM tracks and a failure stores `errno`
  ([IR_COOKBOOK.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#lstatownermodesync-geteuid-and-isexecutablesync)).
- **Globals, and not in a `nish:` module** yet, as `secureZero` is.

The TypeScript reading ([wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §2) is
**class A**: `runtime/nish.mjs` supplies `fs.lstatSync`'s `uid` and `mode`
packed the same way as a BigInt, `process.geteuid()`, and `fs.accessSync` with
`X_OK`, and `owner_checks` prints the same lines under the prelude as natively.

## Secrets: `nish:secret`

Key material is a `Secret<T>`: an opaque value that the checker keeps from
leaving the program by any road but one, and that is zeroed, with a store no
optimiser may remove, before the function that made it lets go of it.

Reference: [`nish:secret`](../nish-secret.md).

| Export | Meaning | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Secret<T>` | an opaque class holding an array or record of integers | `secret_wipe`, `secret_flow`; `reject_secret_shape` |
| `secret(v)` | `v`, which nothing else holds, wrapped; a local is moved | `secret_flow`, `secret_inferred`; `reject_secret_moved`, `reject_secret_unmovable`, `reject_secret_alias_*`, `reject_secret_inferred_*` |
| `expose(s, f)` | `f(value)`, under the rules below | `secret_wipe`; `reject_secret_expose_*` |
| `exposeWith(s, arg, f)` | `f(value, arg)`, under the same rules | `secret_wipe`; `reject_secret_expose_writes_arg` |
| `wipe(x)` | zero a `Secret`, or an array or record of integers `expose`'s function holds | `secret_wipe`, `secret_wipe_o2`, `secret_wipe_o2_inferred`; `reject_secret_wipe_shape`, `reject_secret_wipe_nullable` |

`nish:secret` is the one builtin module with source behind it: `std/secret.ts`,
loaded like a standard-library module, imported only by the builtin name
(`` `nish/secret` is the builtin module `nish:secret` ``, NL2453,
`reject_secret_std_spelling`) and copied, as `std/collections.ts` is, into each
module that uses it, so it writes no `.ll` of its own. `runtime/nish.d.ts`
declares it for `tsc`, with a private constructor and field so that `tsc`
refuses `new Secret` and `s.value` too. Under Node (`runtime/nish.mjs`) a
`Secret` is a plain wrapper and `wipe` zero-fills it.

**A `Secret` local needs no annotation.** `const k = secret(v)` gives `k` the
type `secret` answers, `Secret<T>` for the `T` that `v` is, and every rule
below holds for it as for `const k: Secret<T> = secret(v)`: the payload's
shape, the move and the second reference, each judged where `v` is written
(`secret_inferred` binds an array literal, `new Array`, a call, a moved local,
a ternary, a record and a class unannotated; `reject_secret_inferred_literal`,
`_alias`, `_call`, `_field` and `_moved_class` are refused unannotated as
annotated). The same holds for any generic an imported module declares:
`const b = box(7)` holds the `Box<i32>` that `box` answers, whose layout comes
with the call (`tests/link/generic_import_inferred`), with its methods even
where the module already held `Box<i32>` as a type argument
(`tests/link/generic_import_inferred_held`), and with those of every struct
its fields reach, through an array, a nullable, a `Result` or a nested
instance, in either order (`tests/link/generic_import_inferred_closure`).

**What a `Secret` may hold.** One run of integers, so that `wipe` reaches every
byte with one store: `` `Secret<string>` is not key material `` (NL2428,
`reject_secret_shape`). `wipe` takes a `Secret`, never a nullable one (narrow it
first), or an array or record of integers, and anything else is
`` `wipe` zeroes a `Secret`, or an array or record of integers, and `string` is neither ``
(NL2438, `reject_secret_wipe_shape`, `reject_secret_wipe_nullable`).

**Where a `Secret` may not go.** Each place is refused at the point it is
written, before the general rule it would also break, so the one diagnostic
names the secret:

- a template literal hole (NL2431, `reject_secret_template`);
- an argument of any builtin — `console.log`, a file write, `nish:net`, a
  process, an environment read, `crypto.getRandomValues` — named or imported
  (`` `console.log` cannot be handed a `Secret` ``, NL2432,
  `reject_secret_console`, `reject_secret_file_write`, `reject_secret_net_write`);
- `===` and `!==` against anything but another `Secret` or `null` (NL2433,
  `reject_secret_equality`): `k === null` is how a nullable one narrows;
- the condition of an `if`, a loop or a ternary (NL2434, `reject_secret_condition`);
- an index, as the receiver or as the index (NL2435, `reject_secret_index`,
  `reject_secret_as_index`);
- a member read, written or called anywhere but `std/secret.ts` (NL2436,
  `reject_secret_member`), and `new Secret` (NL2437, `reject_secret_new`);
- an array element, a `Result` payload, or a type argument of any class,
  `Map` and `Set` included (NL2429, `reject_secret_array`,
  `reject_secret_result`, `reject_secret_generic_class`). A `Secret` lives in a
  local, a parameter, or a holder's field ([A `Secret` field](#a-secret-field)),
  and `Secret<T> | null` is how a function hands back one it may not have. Any
  other field — of an interface, of a generic class, not `readonly`, or not
  exactly `Secret<T>` — is NL2430 (`reject_secret_field`,
  `reject_secret_field_interface`, `_generic_class`, `_not_readonly`,
  `_nullable`).

**A `Secret` leaves the function that made it returned or wiped, on every
path.** This is Result rule 1's analysis in its two places — the statement that
drops a value, and the body that never handles one — with the second walked
path by path rather than counted, because "wiped on one arm of an `if`" is not
"wiped" (`reject_secret_one_branch`):

- A `Secret` a call makes has an owner: a `const` or `let`, a `return`, or
  `wipe`. Anywhere else — a statement, a call's argument — it is
  `` `Secret<u8[]>` is made here and nobody owns it `` (NL2439,
  `reject_secret_discarded`, `reject_secret_temporary`).
- Every `return`, `break`, `continue` and `orReturn()` that leaves a `Secret`
  the function made neither wiped nor returned is
  `` `k` holds a `Secret<u8[]>` that this exit leaves neither wiped nor returned `` (NL2440,
  `reject_secret_unwiped_return`, `reject_secret_break`, `reject_secret_or_return`),
  and a block that can reach its end with one is NL2441 (`reject_secret_scope_end`).
  A branch that proves the local `null` (`if (k === null)`) holds none, a
  `panic` or `process.exit` ends the process and the key with it, and a loop is
  walked to its fixpoint, so a `wipe` inside a loop that may run no pass does not
  count (`secret_flow`).
- A `Secret` local may not be assigned while it still holds one (NL2442,
  `reject_secret_overwrite`), read once any path has wiped it (NL2443,
  `reject_secret_after_wipe`), or copied: `const j = k` moves `k` when the
  function made it, and `k` is not read again (NL2446, `reject_secret_moved_out`),
  but a parameter, an element of an array literal or an arm of a ternary is a
  second name for one key (NL2444, `reject_secret_copy_param`).
- `secret(v)` takes a value nothing else holds, and moves it, because a
  second name for the bytes would read the key outside the `Secret`, and
  zeros once `wipe` has run. A local handed in is not read again (NL2445,
  `reject_secret_moved`, whose message says the plain array, and
  `reject_secret_inferred_moved_class` and `reject_secret_moved_interface`,
  where it names the class or interface the plain value is), and neither is
  the local in either arm of `secret(c ? a : b)`. A parameter, a field or an element,
  whose owner keeps the plain bytes, is refused (NL2447,
  `reject_secret_unmovable`). Everything else is judged where it is written:
  - an array or object literal, `null`, and a ternary of fresh values are
    fresh, and so is a `new` whose constructor keeps no `this`;
  - a call is fresh when its callee answers a fresh value, judged over the
    callee's own body by this same rule, through every depth of calls (a
    recursive one included); `expose` and `exposeWith` answer what the
    function they run answers, and `r.orReturn()`, `r.expect(m)` and
    `r.unwrapOr(d)` what `r` carries in its `Ok` (`d` too, which may not be a
    local here, since the move does not reach it). A method of a value,
    `rows.pop()`, may answer what the value holds;
  - a local is fresh when it is the sole reference to its value: every value
    it is given is fresh (another local is not, because that local still
    names it), it is not a `for...of` binding, which names an element, and no
    other use of it leaves a second name. Reading an integer element or field,
    `.length`, an array method on it, `===`, iterating over it, `wipe`, and
    handing it to a builtin, or to a function or method the whole-program
    facts say keeps nothing of it, are all such uses. An initialiser, an
    assignment's value, a field or element store, a literal's element, a
    ternary arm, either side of `??`, the argument of `Ok` or `Err`, an
    assignment to it used as a value (`alias = raw = [1]`, `xs.push(raw =
    [1])`; one whose value is dropped, as a statement or in a `for` header,
    is not), a later declarator of the same statement, a `return`, an argument of a method of
    another value (`rows.push(raw)`, `m.set(k, raw)`), a read by an arrow
    that captures it (a data-parallel body or a spawned task), and a function or constructor
    that keeps it each leave one.

  Each is `` `secret` takes a value nothing else holds, and `raw` has a second
  reference: `const alias = raw` (line 6) ``, naming the reference and its
  line, or the callee and its parameter that keep it (NL2512,
  `reject_secret_alias_const`, `reject_secret_alias_let`,
  `reject_secret_alias_reassigned`, `reject_secret_alias_assign_chain`,
  `_assign_init`, `_assign_push`, `_assign_field`, `_assign_kept`,
  `_assign_helper`, `_assign_parents`, `_assign_constructor`,
  `_assign_source`, `reject_secret_alias_declarators`,
  `reject_secret_alias_field`, `reject_secret_alias_element`,
  `reject_secret_alias_param`,
  `reject_secret_alias_return`, `reject_secret_alias_mutual`,
  `reject_secret_alias_ternary`, `reject_secret_alias_nullish`,
  `reject_secret_alias_ok`, `reject_secret_alias_err`,
  `reject_secret_alias_unwrap_or`, `reject_secret_alias_unwrap_helper`,
  `reject_secret_alias_unwrap_local`, `reject_secret_alias_constructor`,
  `reject_secret_alias_receiver`, `reject_secret_alias_pop`,
  `reject_secret_alias_for_of`, and `reject_secret_alias_capture_map`,
  `_from`, `_map_into`, `_reduce` and `_spawn`, and
  `reject_secret_alias_spawn_arg` and `_spawn_with` for a task's argument,
  which the scope keeps until the task has run). Pass a fresh value instead, or a copy: `const copy: u8[] = new Array<u8>(raw.length);
  copy.set(raw)`, then `secret(copy)`. A declarator that reads `raw` after
  `secret(raw)` in the same statement is a moved read, NL2445
  (`reject_secret_alias_declarator_moved`). The rule refuses some programs
  that are safe, each with the reference named: a data-parallel arrow that
  reads the local before the move, a `Result` local copied into another
  (`reject_secret_alias_result_copy`), and a `let` given another local even
  after the move (`reject_secret_alias_reassigned_after`).
- A `Secret` parameter is borrowed. The callee may read it through `expose`
  or hand it on, and owes nothing: the caller wipes what it made. It neither
  returns it, which would give the caller a second name for a key it already
  owns (NL2546, `reject_secret_field_launder_function` and its siblings, among
  them `reject_secret_field_launder_local` for a caller's own local), nor
  wipes it, which would leave the caller reading zeroes and wiping it again
  (NL2548, `reject_secret_field_wipe_param` and its siblings, among them
  `reject_secret_field_wipe_param_local`). The cases are listed under
  [A `Secret` field](#a-secret-field).

  **This narrows 0.18.0.** Up to 0.18.0 a callee could also return or wipe a
  borrowed `Secret`; from the release after it, both are refused, for every
  `Secret` parameter and not only a holder's field. A function that returned
  its parameter is called for its effect and the caller goes on using the key
  it passed; a function that wiped its parameter leaves the wipe to the owner,
  the function or holder that made the key.

### A `Secret` field

A key that lives as long as an object does — a connection's traffic secret, a
signer's private scalar — is kept in a `readonly` field of exactly `Secret<T>`,
in a class with no type parameters. Such a class is a *holder*. The checker
proves three things of it: the field is set once, from a fresh value; it is
read only where the key cannot get out; and the holder's `wipe()` ends it.

```ts
class Session {
  readonly key: Secret<u8[]>;
  constructor() {
    this.key = secret(new Array<u8>(32));   // once, from a fresh value
  }
  rekey(by: u8): void {
    exposeWith(this.key, by, refill);       // rewritten in place, never replaced
  }
  wipe(): void {
    wipe(this.key);                         // every field, on every path
  }
}
```

- **The releaser.** A holder declares `wipe(): void`, taking no parameters
  (`` `Holder` holds the `Secret` field `k`, so it declares `wipe(): void` ``,
  NL2540, `reject_secret_field_no_wipe`, `_wipe_signature`). Its body calls
  `wipe(this.f)` itself for every `Secret` field, on every path: the field is
  walked as an owned local would be, so a `return` before it, one arm of an
  `if`, a loop that may run no pass, and a helper method that wipes it are each
  `` `this.k` can leave this `wipe()` unwiped `` (NL2541,
  `reject_secret_field_wipe_missing`, `_wipe_return`, `_wipe_branch`,
  `_wipe_loop`, `_wipe_helper`, and `_wipe_new`, where a constructor `new`
  reaches zeroes the key in place). That method is the only place a field
  ends: `wipe(h.f)` anywhere else — a function, another method, a
  constructor, or a function the constructor hands `this` to or stores it
  for — is `` `k` is wiped outside its holder's `wipe()` `` (NL2547,
  `reject_secret_field_wipe_outside`, `_wipe_through`, `_wipe_method`,
  `_wipe_ctor`, `_this_fin`, `_this_store`); call the holder's `wipe()`.
- **Construction.** The field is set in the constructor, by `this.f =
  secret(v)` and nothing else, and `v` is judged by the sole-reference rule
  above (NL2512, `reject_secret_field_alias_raw`). A parameter, a call that
  answers a `Secret`, or a local holding one is
  `` `this.k` is set from something other than `secret(...)` `` (NL2542,
  `reject_secret_field_param`, `_call`, `_local`); a second store while the
  first may still be there, a later loop pass included, is NL2543
  (`reject_secret_field_twice`, `_ctor_loop`). The field is `readonly`, so a
  store anywhere else — a method, a function, a compound `+=`, or a second
  name for `this` — is the `readonly` refusal, NL2181
  (`reject_secret_field_store_method`, `_store_outside`, `_compound`,
  `_this_escape`). The store is a statement of its own: `const x = (this.k =
  secret(v))` binds the key a second time, and is NL2544
  (`reject_secret_field_store_value`). A holder is made only by `new`: an
  object literal is NL2545 (`reject_secret_field_object_literal`), and typed
  JSON neither encodes nor decodes one (NL2485, `reject_secret_field_json`, `_json_decode`).
- **Reads.** `h.f` is borrowed, as a `Secret` parameter is: it is an argument
  of a call or a `new` — `expose`, `exposeWith`, or a function that
  takes a `Secret`, and `wipe` only in the holder's own `wipe()` (NL2547) — or an operand of `===` or `!==` against another `Secret`
  (a field is never `null`, so `h.k === null` is a type error, NL2024). Bound to a local, assigned, returned, chosen by a ternary or `??`,
  or read through `?.` or a chain of fields, it would be a second owner of the
  key, and is `` `k` is a `Secret` field, which is read only as a call's
  argument or an `===`/`!==` operand `` (NL2544, `reject_secret_field_bind`,
  `_assign_local`, `_return`, `_ternary`, `_nullish`, `_optional_chain`,
  and `_nested` for `o.h.k`; `_chain` is the chained store `this.k = this.j =
  secret(v)`). What a borrow receives stays borrowed: a function, an arrow or
  a generic `id<T>` that takes a `Secret` and returns it would hand the
  caller a second name for the holder's key, and is
  `` `s` is a `Secret` parameter, which its caller owns and wipes: returned ``
  (NL2546, `reject_secret_field_launder_function`, `_launder_arrow`,
  `_launder_generic`, `_launder_method`, and `_launder_local` for a caller's
  own local); one that wipes it is NL2548 (`reject_secret_field_wipe_param`,
  `_wipe_param_new`, `_wipe_param_method`, and `_wipe_param_local` for a
  caller's own local). A ternary that picks one of two borrowed parameters to
  return is refused before it gets there, as a copy (NL2444,
  `reject_secret_field_launder_ternary`). Every place a `Secret` may not go is closed to the field too:
  `reject_secret_field_console` (NL2432), `_template` (NL2431), `_equality`
  (NL2433), `_condition` (NL2434), `_index` (NL2435), `_member` (NL2436),
  `_array`, `_array_literal` and `_result` (NL2429), `_new_arg` (NL2439: a
  `Secret` made for a constructor that keeps none, beside an accepted
  `new Box(h.k)` that borrows the field), and `_secret_arg` and
  `_holder_payload` (NL2428: neither a `Secret` nor a holder is key material).
- **The holder is a value.** It may be aliased and kept in an array, a `Map`,
  another object's field or a `Result`. The rules that follow are the general
  ones, applied to a holder as to any class: a data-parallel body may not
  capture one (NL2504, `reject_secret_field_capture`) nor may a task (NL2509,
  `_task_wipe`), the scope's own thread may not wipe one a task of it may read
  before the join — through `wipe()`, a helper or a constructor
  (`_scope_wipe`, `_scope_helper`, `_scope_new`) — and `using` does not take
  one (NL2387, `reject_secret_field_using`).

`secret_field` runs all of it, and `tests/run.js` holds the wipe to `-O2`
("nish:secret: a holder's wipe survives opt -O2"): `secret_field_wipe_o2`'s
`wipe()` is a volatile `llvm.memset` of the key after `opt -O2`, where its twin
`secret_field_wipe_o2_plain`, zeroing the same bytes with `fill(0)`, has an
ordinary one. An exported holder appears in an `--emit-header` sidecar as an
opaque struct, a `typedef` with no fields: with its layout a host could
allocate one and skip the constructor that sets the key, so it reaches C only
as a pointer. A `Secret` an exported function takes or returns is likewise a
pointer to an opaque struct, as a `Map` is, and `--emit-dts` and `--emit-napi`
bridge no function that takes or returns a holder or a `Secret`
("nish:secret: --emit-header keeps a Secret and its holder opaque, and
--emit-dts / --emit-napi bridge neither").

What the rule leaves out, so a review need not look for it here:

- **A holder nobody wipes.** The checker proves that `wipe()` ends every key,
  not that anybody calls it: a holder dropped, or released with its arena,
  without `wipe()` leaves its key in memory. Holders are values that cross
  functions, aliases and containers, and their owner is not tracked.
- **Aliases.** `wipe()` through one alias zeroes the key for every alias, and
  an `expose` through another reads zeros afterwards: a wrong answer, never a
  leak.
- **Plain temporaries.** What an exposed function copies out of the key is a
  plain value, and is wiped only if that function wipes it.
- **Per-packet and per-record keys.** These cannot be a `Secret` under today's
  `expose`: sealing writes the output buffer (NL2450) and the AES kernels are C
  (NL2448).

**`expose` and `exposeWith`.** The function either runs is a
[function parameter](declarations.md#function-parameters): a top-level function named at the
call, or an arrow written there. It is judged once the whole-program facts are
in, at the call, and what it returns is the only thing that leaves:

- It reaches no I/O — no builtin that touches a file, a directory, a process,
  the environment, a socket, a stream, the clock or entropy — and no C, through
  any depth of calls (`` `leak` reaches `writeFileSync` through `store` ``,
  NL2448, `reject_secret_expose_io`, `reject_secret_expose_io_deep`,
  `reject_secret_expose_c`). A `panic` or exit is allowed only with a literal,
  since a computed message or status is output (`reject_secret_expose_panic`).
  A failed runtime check — an index, a slice, a division — still stops the
  program with its message, which carries the operand it failed on; an index
  that depends on a key is already a cache-timing defect, and is for the
  constant-time checks of WP34 N6 to find.
- It keeps nothing of the value: returning it, storing it or passing it where
  it is kept is NL2449 (`reject_secret_expose_keeps`). `exposeWith`'s function
  writes nothing through the argument it is handed either (NL2450,
  `reject_secret_expose_writes_arg`), which would be a road out its result type
  does not name.
- Its result is a declared type that holds no `Secret` (NL2451,
  `reject_secret_expose_secret_result`), and an arrow writes that type down
  (NL2452, `reject_secret_expose_undeclared`).

**The wipe.** Each `wipe` instance is one `llvm.memset` with its volatile flag
set, over an array's whole capacity — a `pop` leaves the old element in the
buffer — or a record's `sizeof`. LLVM never removes, merges or narrows a
volatile memory intrinsic, so the store survives every optimisation, inlining
included: `tests/run.js` compiles `secret_wipe_o2`, whose wiped bytes nothing
reads again, beside a twin that zeroes them with `fill(0)`, and after
`opt -O2` the twin holds no store and the wipe holds one volatile zero per byte.
`secret_wipe_o2_inferred` does the same for a `Secret` bound with no
annotation, beside `secret_wipe_o2_inferred_plain` ("nish:secret: an inferred
`Secret`'s wipe survives opt -O2 (a volatile memset of its key), where the
twin's fill(0) is deleted").
Two things it does not reach, and says so: a buffer a `push` outgrew, which is
no longer the array's, and a string, which is immutable and is not key material.

`wipe` and [`secureZero`](#wiping-a-secret-securezero) both make a store no
optimisation removes, and differ in what they take and where the store is
written. `secureZero` is a global over a bare `u8[]`, one call into the C
runtime; `wipe` is the `Secret`'s own, takes any integer width or a record of
integers, and is an intrinsic emitted into the program, so it needs no runtime
function and works wherever the program's IR does. Key material belongs in a
`Secret`, and `secureZero` is for bytes that never were one.

## Regions: `nish:region`

A region is memory a program frees when it says so: an arena of its own,
reached through a handle. A long-running program — a cache, a server's
per-connection state — keeps each thing that lives and dies together in one
region and gives the whole of it back with one `free`, where the thread's arena
would hold it until the program ends.

Reference: [`nish:region`](../nish-region.md).

| Export | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Region<T>` | a handle to a region whose root is a `T`: a 64-bit number, not a pointer |
| `region(f)`, `regionWith(arg, f)` | a new region, whose root is what `f` answers; `f`'s allocations land in it |
| `enter(r, f)`, `enterWith(r, arg, f)` | `f(root)` (or `f(root, arg)`), allocating in the region |
| `free(r)` | gives the region's memory back; `r` and every copy of it are dead |

`f` is an arrow or a named function, and an arrow captures nothing (NL2335),
so the ways into a region are its root, `arg` and module state. The checker
follows each (`src/region-rules.ts`), with two kinds of value: *region memory*
(the root, and whatever `f` allocates) and *outer memory* (`arg`, module state,
what a callee answers from outside). A number, a `boolean`, an `enum` and a
`Region` are copied, never pointed at, so they cross freely
(`tests/cases/region_cache`).

| Refused | Code |
| --- | --- |
| region memory stored into outer memory: a field or an element, including `this` stored by a constructor `f` reaches (`h.l = this`). Module state cannot hold region memory at all, since a module binding is a number, `boolean` or string constant or [module storage](declarations.md#module-storage), whose elements are pointer-free, and a top-level `let` is refused first (`reject_region_ctor_module_state`) | **NL2609** (`reject_region_to_outer`, `reject_region_ctor_this_arg`, `reject_region_store_string`, `reject_region_arrow_keep`, `reject_region_arrow_generic`) |
| outer memory that is not a number, `boolean`, `enum` or string literal stored into region memory: a field or element store, a constructor argument (`new Game(g.host)`) or a field of a literal | **NL2610** (`reject_region_outer_string_ctor`, `reject_region_outer_string_literal`, `reject_region_arrow_link`, `reject_region_arrow_result`, `reject_region_arrow_compose`, `reject_region_arrow_twice`, `reject_region_fixpoint_chain`) |
| `enter`'s or `enterWith`'s `f` answering anything but a number, a `boolean`, an `enum` or a `Region`: an array, an object or a string | **NL2611** (`reject_region_enter_result`, `reject_region_enter_string`) |
| `scope()`, `spawn`, a parallel body or a channel inside `f`, directly or through a callee | **NL2612** (`reject_region_threads`) |
| a value whose type holds a `Region` at any depth crossing to another thread: a task's argument or answer, a parallel body's capture, a value sent on a channel | **NL2613** (`reject_region_task_arg_field`, `reject_region_task_answer`, `reject_region_channel_map`, `reject_region_parallel_capture`) |
