| `region`'s or `regionWith`'s `f` answering anything but memory it allocated: `region(() => moduleValue)`, `regionWith(g, (a) => a)` | **NL2614** (`reject_region_root_module`, `reject_region_root_arg`) |
| outer storage growing inside `f`, directly or through a callee: `push` on an outer array (arrays have no `unshift` or `splice`; the rule names them so it holds if they come), `Map.set` or `Set.add` on an outer `Map` or `Set` | **NL2615** (`reject_region_grow_push`, `reject_region_grow_map`, `reject_region_grow_set`, each with a `_callee` twin, `reject_region_arrow_grow`) |
| a call inside `f` the region rules have no facts for. No program reaches it today, since every function, instantiation, lifted arrow and `declare function` has whole-program facts; it stays so that such a callee is never let through unexamined (`tests/wordings/unreachable.txt`) | **NL2616** |
| `Arena.mark` or `Arena.used` inside `f`, or a callee reaching one: inside a region they would read the region's own arena, not the thread's | **NL2617** (`reject_region_arena_mark` through `region`, `reject_region_arena_used_callee` through `enter` and a callee) |
| `new Region<T>()` | **NL2618** (`reject_region_new`) |
| `region`, `regionWith`, `enter`, `enterWith` or `free` in a parallel body or a spawned function, directly or through a callee | NL2351 (`reject_region_enter_spawned`, `reject_region_parallel_callee`) |
| `using r = region(f)`, in any declarator: a block does not free a region | NL2387 (`reject_region_using_first`, `reject_region_using_second`) |

- **`Arena.mark` and `Arena.used` are refused inside `f`** (NL2617). Inside a
  region they read the region's arena, not the thread's, so a mark taken there
  names nothing the thread's arena knows once `f` returns
  (`docs/security/runtime.md`, RT-45).
- **An arrow handed to a function runs inside `f`, and is judged as `f`'s
  own code.** Its body is walked with what it captures, its parameters take
  what the call is handed, what any arrow of the same call answers (the callee
  may feed one arrow's answer to another, or to itself) or memory the callee
  allocated, and what it answers is part of what the call answers, so
  `pick(() => a.node)` stored in the root is NL2610 as `a.node` is
  (`reject_region_arrow_keep`, `_grow`, `_link`, `_result`, `_generic`,
  `_compose`, `_compose_temp`, `_twice`, `_twice_temp`). The walk runs to a fixpoint however long a chain of
  assignments is, never a fixed number of rounds (`reject_region_fixpoint_chain`).
- **The rules are on types for threads, on values inside `f`.** NL2613 follows
  the type, so a handle hidden in a field of a task's argument is caught where
  it crosses, whatever route brought it there. A handle stored in region
  memory, or answered by `enter`, stays on its thread and is allowed.
- `using a = arena()` inside `f` is allowed, and so is `enter` of a second
  region: only numbers come out of it.
- **Every call checks its handle at run time.** `enter`, `enterWith` and
  `free` stop the program on a handle that is 0, freed already, or another
  thread's; `enter` of a region already entered and `free` of an entered one
  stop it too, so freeing twice is a panic and never a double free. Each call
  is a `region` site under [`--deny-panics`](semantics-decisions.md#panic-sites)
  (`reject_deny_panics_region`), and no proof removes it. Past 16,777,216 live
  regions `region` stops the program as well.
- A program run under Node as it is written (`runtime/nish.mjs`) gets a
  region as an entry in a table, `free` drops it, and the same handle checks
  throw. `--emit-ts` output is different: the runtime it imports
  (`nish/runtime`) has no regions yet, so it refuses the module (NL4015,
  `reject_emit_ts_region`).

## `process`

The reference for each member of `process`, with its parameters, its answer and its capability, is its doc comment in [`runtime/nish.d.ts`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/runtime/nish.d.ts); the rules are here.

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `process.exit(code: i32): void` | `nish_exit` -> libc `exit(code)` (stdio buffers of linked C code are flushed; the arena is abandoned); statement position; a terminator | write, `noreturn` | `process_exit`, `reject_exit_unreachable` |
| `process.argv: string[]` | the command line: `process.argv[0]` is the program path (C's `argv[0]`, one index earlier than Node, whose `argv[0]` is the `node` binary and `argv[1]` the script) and the rest are the arguments as UTF-8 byte strings; read-only | read | `argv_echo` (run with `argv_echo.argv`), `link/argv_import`; `reject_argv_assign`, `reject_argv_push` (`` `process.argv` is read-only ``) |
| `process.platform: string` | the operating system the **program** is running on, spelled as Node spells it: `"linux"`, `"darwin"`, or `"unknown"` for anything this compiler has no target triple for (every WASI build included) | none | `io_host`; `reject_platform_assign` (`` Cannot assign to `process.platform` ``) |
| `process.arch: string` | the architecture, likewise: `"x64"`, `"arm64"`, or `"unknown"` | none | `io_host`; `reject_arch_call` (`` Unknown builtin `process.arch` ``) |

`process.platform` and `process.arch` are what `--target host` asks the
machine (WP14 §7a): the pair maps to `x86_64`/`aarch64` plus
`-unknown-linux-gnu`/`-apple-darwin`, and anything else means this compiler has
no triple for the host and says so. Each is one call to the runtime, which
answers the address of a string in its own constant data — settled when
`runtime.c` was compiled, so a cross build reports the *target*, and nothing is
allocated or loaded, which is why the declarations are `readnone` and a
function built only from these stays pure. They carry no rule about the entry
point, unlike `process.argv` below: there is nothing for a wrapper to build, so
a wasm or N-API library may read them too. Neither can be assigned to.

`process.argv` is an ordinary `string[]` value (`length`, `a[i]`, `for...of`,
passing it to functions, aliasing it with `const args = process.argv`) that
the `@main` wrapper builds once with `nish_argv_init(argc, argv)` before the
program runs; every module of the program may read it, and each read is one
`load` of the runtime global `@nish_argv` (a memory read: the function is at
most `readonly`). The array lives outside the arena, so no arena scope's
release invalidates it. Storing into it (`process.argv[i] = s`, `op=`,
`++`/`--`, `push`) is rejected. A program without `export const main`, as
for a wasm or N-API library, has nothing to build it from and rejects every
use with `` `process.argv` requires a `main` entry point `` (`reject_argv_no_main`,
`tests/link/argv_no_main`). Under the `wasi` build profile the WASI host
supplies the arguments (`examples/wasi-host.mjs`).

Reference: [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

## File I/O

Reference: [`nish:fs`](../nish-fs.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `readFileSync(path: string): string` | whole file as one arena string; failure prints `nish: cannot read <path>` to stderr and exits 1 | write | `io_files`; `reject_readfile_number` (`` `readFileSync` expects an argument of type string, got i32 ``) |
| `readFileSyncOrNull(path: string): string \| null` | the same read, `null` where the other exits (WP14 B3): `null` for exactly the set of paths `readFileSync` prints `nish: cannot read <path>` for, a **directory** included. The result is narrowed with `if (text !== null)` like any other nullable | write | `io_streams`; `reject_readfile_or_null_unchecked` |
| `readFileBytesSync(path: string): u8[] \| null` | the file's **bytes**, as they are on disk, or `null` for exactly the paths `readFileSyncOrNull` answers `null` for; there is no exiting twin. An ordinary arena `u8[]` with `length === capacity`, narrowed with `if (b !== null)`. A `wasm32` build has no `readFileBytesSync`, as it has no `readFileSync`. The TypeScript reading is class A (WP34 N2) | write | `bytes_read`, `bytes_read_import`, `mem_read_bytes_scope`; `reject_bytes_read_unchecked`, `reject_bytes_read_arity` (NL2061), `reject_bytes_read_type` (NL2268) |
| `writeFileSync(path: string, data: string): void` | create/truncate (`0644`) and write; statement position. A symbolic link as the last component of `path` is refused (`nish: cannot write <path>`), where Node follows it | write | `io_files` |
| `appendFileSync(path: string, data: string): void` | create/append and write; statement position. A symbolic link as the last component is refused, as for `writeFileSync` | write | `io_files` |
| `writeFileBytesSync(path: string, bytes: readonly u8[]): i32` | create/truncate (`0644`) and write the array's bytes as they are. A symbolic link as the last component is refused (`-40` ELOOP). Where `writeFileSync` exits, this **answers** `bytes.length` or a negative errno, never a panic | write | `io_write_file_bytes`, `io_write_bytes`; `reject_write_file_bytes_arity`, `reject_write_file_bytes_type` (NL2268), `reject_write_file_bytes_wasm` |
| `renameSync(from: string, to: string): i32` | `rename(2)`: `from` replaces `to` in one step, so a reader sees the old file or the new one and never neither. `0`, or a negative errno; `-18` **EXDEV** across file systems, since nothing is copied. Never a panic | write | `io_rename`, `caps_fs_replace`; `reject_rename_arity`, `reject_rename_type`, `reject_rename_wasm` |
| `unlinkSync(path: string): i32` | `unlink(2)`: removes the name, and a symbolic link itself rather than what it names. A **directory is refused** (`-21` EISDIR on Linux, `-1` EPERM where the kernel answers so), with no fallback to `rmdir`. `0`, or a negative errno. Never a panic | write | `io_unlink`, `caps_fs_replace`; `reject_unlink_arity`, `reject_unlink_type`, `reject_unlink_wasm` |
| `writeFileSyncMode(path: string, data: string, mode: i32): i32` | `writeFileSync` with the file left at exactly `mode`: an `fchmod(2)` sets it **before the first byte is written**, so the umask cannot widen it and a wider existing file is narrowed before it holds the new contents. A descriptor opened before is not revoked. The file is written **in place**: a failure leaves it empty or partial, and a file this process may write but does not own is emptied before `-1` EPERM, so a secret that replaces another goes through a temporary and `renameSync`. A symbolic link as the last component is refused (`-40` ELOOP), its target untouched. A mode outside `0..0o777` is `-22` (the setuid, setgid and sticky bits are refused, not applied). The length written, or a negative errno. Never a panic | write | `io_write_file_mode`, `caps_fs_mode`, `fs_mode` (modes read back by `stat`, umask `022` and `077`); `reject_write_file_mode_arity`, `reject_write_file_mode_type`, `reject_write_file_mode_wasm` |
| `createFileExclusiveSync(path: string, data: string, mode: i32): i32` | `O_CREAT\|O_EXCL` at exactly `mode`, set as for `writeFileSyncMode`: `-17` **EEXIST** when any name is already there, a dangling symbolic link included, which is never followed. Exactly one of any number of racing processes wins, so it is a lock file; a winner whose write fails removes the file before it answers. The length written, or a negative errno. Never a panic | write | `io_create_exclusive`, `fs_mode` (eight children race, one wins; a failed write leaves no file); `reject_create_exclusive_arity`, `reject_create_exclusive_type`, `reject_create_exclusive_mode_type`, `reject_create_exclusive_wasm` |
| `mkdirSyncMode(path: string, mode: i32): i32` | `mkdir(2)` of one level at `mode`, with the process umask applied. An existing name is `-17` EEXIST, its mode never changed; a mode outside `0..0o777` (the sticky, setuid and setgid bits included) is `-22`. `0`, or a negative errno. Never a panic | write | `io_mkdir_mode`, `caps_fs_mode`, `fs_mode`; `reject_mkdir_mode_arity`, `reject_mkdir_mode_type`, `reject_mkdir_mode_mode_type`, `reject_mkdir_mode_wasm` |

The ones that answer an `i32` answer the platform's errno values,
untranslated, and the same numbers under Node; the ones shown here are
Linux's, so compare against a negative result. A `wasm32` build has none of
these, and a WASI build answers `-ENOSYS` from the three that take a mode, as
WASI has no file modes to set.

**Bytes out, and the string route.** A native string is `{len, bytes}`,
never validated as UTF-8, and `write`, `writeError`, `writeFileSync` and
`appendFileSync` send its `len` bytes as they are, so a string built by
`String.fromBytes` from any bytes, all 256 values included, leaves exactly
as it came in (`tests/cases/io_write_bytes`, compared with
`io_write_bytes.bin` byte for byte). That route is native-only. Under the
prelude (`runtime/nish.mjs`) `String.fromBytes` makes each byte one UTF-16
unit, which leaves as UTF-8, so a byte above 127 becomes two; under
`--emit-ts` the bytes decode as UTF-8 and a byte that is not UTF-8 becomes
U+FFFD. `writeBytes` and `writeFileBytesSync` send a `u8[]` as it is on
every host, and are the route for bytes that are not text.

Paths are relative to the working directory. `readFileSync`,
`readFileSyncOrNull` and `readFileBytesSync` treat a file longer than
2^31 − 1 bytes as one they cannot read, in both number modes, which matches
Node. Every path, name and argument a builtin hands the OS that holds a NUL
byte is refused as a missing path is — `null`, `false`, `-1` or
`cannot …`, whichever that builtin answers — where Node refuses it by
throwing ([docs/security/runtime.md](../../security/runtime.md), RT-1, RT-3, RT-4). These are globals, not
`import { readFileSync } from "fs"` (bare imports are rejected), and so are
`write`, `writeError` and `panic` above. A user function of the same name
wins, as it does for every identifier builtin.

## Directories and subprocesses

Reference: [`nish:fs`](../nish-fs.md), [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mkdirSync(path: string): boolean` | create **one** directory, mode `0777 & ~umask`, not recursive, exactly like Node's `fs.mkdirSync(p)` with no options. `true` when a directory exists at `path` once the call returns, whoever made it; `false` for every other outcome, a plain file at `path` included | write | `io_mkdir`; `reject_mkdir_arity`, `reject_mkdir_type` |
| `isDirectorySync(path: string): boolean` | one `stat`: `true` when a directory exists at `path` as the call runs, `false` for everything else. It is the question `-o <dir>` asks of a path, and the `stat` half of `mkdirSync`, which calls it (WP14 §7a) | write | `io_is_directory`; `reject_is_directory_arity`, `reject_is_directory_type` |
| `spawnSync(argv: string[]): number` | run `argv[0]`, searched on `PATH`, and wait for it: its exit status, or `128 + n` when signal `n` killed it (the shell's convention). `-1` for an **empty** vector, a child that cannot be started or waited for, and always on WASI, which has no processes. The child inherits this process's environment, streams and working directory | write | `io_spawn`; `reject_spawn_arity`, `reject_spawn_element_type` |
| `spawnSyncTo(argv: string[], stdoutPath: string, stderrPath: string): number` | the same run, with each stream sent to a file created or truncated at `0644`; an **empty** path leaves that stream inherited, and a symbolic link as a path's last component is refused, which answers `-1`. The two paths must not name one file; capture them apart and concatenate | write | `io_spawn_to`, `io_spawn_to_inherit`; `reject_spawn_to_arity`, `reject_spawn_to_type` |
| `spawnPiped(argv: string[], stdin: readonly u8[], stdout: u8[], stderr: u8[]): i32` | the same run, with every stream a pipe: the child reads `stdin` and then end of file, and its stdout and stderr are **appended** to `stdout` and `stderr`. The status, `128 + n`, or `-1` as for `spawnSync` (and for a failed pipe or `poll`); a stream past **16 MiB** (`NISH_PIPED_CAP`) kills the child with `SIGKILL` and answers `-2`. The child holds no descriptor of the program but its three streams, and the program's SIGPIPE from a child that stopped reading is absorbed. The two output arrays are grown by the runtime, so they are push receivers to the arena analysis, and `readonly` is refused for them, as is a typed-array spelling (`Int32Array`, ...), whose length is fixed | write | `io_spawn_piped`, `mem_spawn_piped_scope`; `reject_spawn_piped_arity`, `reject_spawn_piped_element_type`, `reject_spawn_piped_stdin_type`, `reject_spawn_piped_output`, `reject_spawn_piped_typed_output`, `reject_spawn_piped_wasm`, `reject_using_arena_spawn_piped` |
| `readdirSync(path: string): string[] \| null` | the directory's entries, **sorted ascending by bytes**, without `.` and `..`. `null` when the directory cannot be read at all, a *different* answer from the empty array of an empty directory. A WASI build always answers `null`: `fd_readdir` lists a preopened directory rather than a path, which is a different contract and not a port of this one | write | `io_readdir`, `io_readdir_null`; `reject_readdir_arity`, `reject_readdir_type`, `reject_readdir_unchecked` |
| `realpathSync(path: string): string \| null` | `path` resolved to an **absolute** path with no symbolic link, `.`, `..` or repeated separator, or `null` when it does not resolve. POSIX `realpath` needs every component but the last to exist, so "does not resolve" is one answer rather than several, and the answer the caller asked for rather than an error. Copied into the arena and narrowed with `if (p !== null)` like any other nullable (WP19 §5a item 4) | write | `io_realpath`; `reject_realpath_arity`, `reject_realpath_type` |

All five answer a value where they could have exited, for the reason
`readFileSyncOrNull` answers `null` (WP14 B3): the language has no exceptions,
so a driver has to be able to turn the failure into its own diagnostic. They
exist so that a compiler written in Nish can create its own `-o dir/`,
tell `-o out` meaning a directory from `-o out` meaning a file, and shell out
for `--link` — `mkdirSync` and `spawnSync` are the calls
[wp14-selfhost.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp14-selfhost.md) §3a D4 named as the price of a
self-hosted link step, and `isDirectorySync` is the one §7a named as the price
of the last spelling of `-o` that, at the time, only the TypeScript compiler
handled.

`spawnSync` and `spawnSyncTo` are the two builtins whose pointer argument the
runtime keeps: the spawn path copies each element's bytes pointer into a vector
that outlives the call, so the array escapes, a parameter passed to either is
never `nocapture`, and an array literal handed to one is never stack-allocated
(`io_spawn` pins all three). Nothing that can reach either is `willreturn`
either, because the child may never exit. The argument is checked down to its
element type: an `i32[]` is an array but not a command line
(`reject_spawn_element_type`). Arguments are passed as bytes, so an embedded NUL
truncates one.

`spawnSyncTo` is a second builtin rather than two more parameters on the first
because the language had no default parameters when it was added — and the alternative shape, answering
the output as a string, was refused for two reasons: the runtime would have to
buffer a child that can print more than memory holds, and a harness comparing
output against a golden wants the bytes on disk anyway, to diff and to keep
after a failure.

`spawnPiped` is the run whose streams stay in memory, for a child that takes
a secret: a password manager's or keychain's CLI reads it on stdin, and stdin
is the one place `ps`, `/proc/<pid>/environ` and the file system do not show.
Its shape is four arguments with the outputs as out-parameters, the way
`readBytesInto` fills a caller's array. The rejected shape answered a record
(`{ status, stdout, stderr }`): no builtin returns a class, and there is no
way to declare one the checker, both emitters and the TypeScript prelude would
share, so the record would have been the first and its own construct. The
out-parameters cost a caller two `const out: u8[] = []` lines; they also let a
loop reuse one pair of arrays. The runtime writes `stdin` and drains both
outputs in one `poll` loop, so a child that fills one pipe while the parent
waits on another cannot deadlock it, and the 16 MiB cap is the answer to the
reason `spawnSyncTo` gave for refusing to buffer: a child that prints more
than memory holds is stopped, with a code no exit status can be, rather than
followed (`docs/security/runtime.md`, RT-27 to RT-31).

`spawnWithFds` numbers the descriptors from 3 rather than taking a target
for each, because 3 onward is where a child that is handed descriptors looks
for them (systemd's socket activation, `LISTEN_FDS`), and a target list would
let a program aim one at 0 to 2 and lose the child's streams. The runtime
duplicates each source above the targets before the child's `dup2` reads it,
so an entry that is its own target or another's is never overwritten first
(`docs/security/runtime.md`, RT-40).

`readdirSync` sorts, which neither `readdir(3)` nor Node's `fs.readdirSync`
does, and that is a decision about this language rather than a convenience:
every caller of an unsorted listing would have to sort it before reading it,
and a run whose order is the file system's is a run that
differs between two machines. The sort is by **bytes**, like every other string
comparison here, so it agrees with Node's `.sort()` for ASCII names and can
differ for names that are not (`docs/wp13-differential.md`).

## The environment

Reference: [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `getenv(name: string): string \| null` | the value of environment variable `name` as the call runs, or `null` when it is **unset**; a variable set to nothing (`CC=`) answers a zero-length string. The bytes are copied into the arena, so the result outlives any later change to the environment; it is narrowed with `if (cc !== null)` like any other nullable (WP19 R1) | write | `io_getenv`; `reject_getenv_arity`, `reject_getenv_type`, `reject_getenv_unchecked` |

It is a **call and not `process.env.CC`**, and that is a language decision
rather than a spelling: `process.env.NAME` is member access on a key chosen at
runtime, which Phase 0 forbids outright
([wp19-stage0-retirement.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp19-stage0-retirement.md) §4). The two
`process.*` values the language does have — `process.argv`, and
`process.platform` / `process.arch` below — are fixed names with no key.

`null` and `""` are different answers, and a driver acts on the difference: an
unset `CC` means "use the default", and `CC=` means someone set it to nothing.
That is why the result is `string | null` and not a string that is empty when
nothing is there.

There is no `setenv`: a program can read its environment and pass an
environment on to a child through `spawnSync`, which inherits this process's,
but it cannot change its own. Nothing in the compiler needs to, and a setter
would make `getenv`'s "as the call runs" a much sharper caveat than it is.
Because of that, a test that depends on a variable is given one by the harness
— `tests/cases/<name>.env`, one `NAME=value` per line, read by both
`tests/run.js` and the differential runner so the native binary and the Node
rewrite see the same environment.

Two reads of one variable in a function are two calls: the declaration is not
`readonly`, because a `setenv` from linked C — this program cannot call one,
but a library linked beside it can — may change the answer between them, so
LLVM may not fold the second read into the first.

The value is what `getenv(3)` answers, so it is bytes, and every offset into
it is a byte offset.

## The clock

Reference: [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `monotonicNanos(): i64` | `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` in nanoseconds; the origin is arbitrary, so only the **difference** between two reads means anything | write | `io_monotonic`; `reject_monotonic_arity` |
| `wallClockNanos(): i64` | `CLOCK_REALTIME` in nanoseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC, as an `i64`. It can go backwards when the system time is set, so a duration is `monotonicNanos`'s job. Not refused on wasm, as the monotonic clock is | write | `wall_clock`; `reject_wall_clock_arity` |

It is an `i64` in both number modes and not a `number`, because a `number` is an
`i32` by default and would overflow inside a tenth of a second, and an `f64`
loses nanoseconds after about 104 days of uptime.

It is the **monotonic** clock and not the wall clock, and the type cannot say so,
so the name does. An elapsed time measured from a wall clock has to survive that
clock being corrected mid-run, and it cannot: the difference can come out
negative. The wall clock is `Date.now()`, below, and it is the only part of
`Date` there is: a program that formats a date needs a calendar, a time zone
database and a locale, none of which this language has.

The effect is `write` rather than `none` for the reason `getenv` is not
`readnone`: the clock is not memory LLVM is tracking, so two reads with work
between them must not fold into one. A `readnone` clock would make every measured
interval exactly zero, which `io_monotonic` is the test for.

## The host: the wall clock, entropy, file times and signals

Four facts a program that runs for days asks of the machine (WP34 N3): what time
it is, bytes nobody can predict, whether a file was renewed, and whether it has
been asked to stop. All four are C in `runtime/runtime-host.c`, a translation
unit of its own with its own `.text*` ceiling, which `scripts/build.sh` compiles
beside `runtime.c` as it does the others.

Reference: [`nish:fs`](../nish-fs.md), [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Date.now(): f64` | the wall clock, `CLOCK_REALTIME`, in **whole milliseconds** since 1970-01-01 UTC, as JavaScript answers it: the milliseconds are counted as integers and then converted, so the value is exact and a time before 1970 floors. An `f64` in both number modes, because an `i32` of milliseconds overflowed in January 1970. It can go backwards when the clock is corrected, so an interval is `monotonicNanos`'s job, not this one's | write | `os_now`, `os_now_i32`; `reject_os_date_now_arity` |
| `crypto.getRandomValues(bytes: u8[]): void` | every byte of `bytes` from the kernel's CSPRNG: `getrandom(2)` on Linux, looping over `EINTR` and short reads, and `getentropy(3)` in 256-byte chunks on macOS. **A `u8[]` only**, where the Web API takes any integer typed array: the byte is the unit a key or a nonce is written in, and a wider element would make the answer's byte order a fact about the machine. **A statement**, where the Web API also answers its argument, which the caller already holds. An empty array is filled with nothing. **At most 65,536 bytes a call**, the Web API's limit: more is a panic, `crypto.getRandomValues: <n> bytes asked for, and one call fills at most 65536`, exit 1. A source that fails is a panic too; nothing weaker is ever substituted | write | `os_random`, `os_random_limit`; `reject_os_random_i32`, `reject_os_random_u32`, `reject_os_random_string`, `reject_os_random_readonly`, `reject_os_random_value`, `reject_os_random_arity`, `reject_os_crypto_member`, `reject_os_crypto_value`, `reject_thread_region_random` |
| `statMtimeSync(path: string): f64` | the modification time in milliseconds since the epoch, **with the sub-millisecond fraction** kept, computed as Node's `mtimeMs` is (seconds × 1e3 plus nanoseconds ÷ 1e6, in doubles), so the two print the same digits. **NaN** when the path cannot be stat'd, because an `f64` has no `null` ([Nullable types](types.md#nullable-types)); test it with `m !== m`. `stat` follows a symbolic link, and a directory has a time of its own. Also exported by `nish:fs` | write | `os_mtime`, `os_mtime_import`; `reject_os_mtime_type`, `reject_os_mtime_arity`, `reject_os_mtime_nullable` |
| `signalFd(): i32` | a descriptor that becomes readable when **SIGTERM or SIGINT** arrives: the read end of a pipe a `sigaction` handler writes one byte to per signal, so the signals' default action never runs. The handler runs in whichever thread the signal lands on, so a `scope()` task or a parallel worker running when `signalFd()` is called cannot take the signal and end the process, and nothing is blocked for a spawned child to inherit. It overrides a disposition the process started with, as `process.on("SIGTERM")` does under Node. Made **once**; `-1` when it cannot be made. Also exported by `nish:process` | write | `os_signal`, `os_signal_import`; `reject_os_signal_fd_arity` |
| `readSignal(fd: i32): i32` | block until one of the two signals arrives and answer **15** or **2**; `-1` for an `fd` that is not `signalFd()`'s and for a read that fails. The argument is an `i32` in both number modes, and an `f64`, an `i64` or a string is refused rather than converted. Not `willreturn`. Also exported by `nish:process` | write | `os_signal`, `os_signal_import`; `reject_os_signal_f64`, `reject_os_signal_i64`, `reject_os_signal_string`, `reject_os_signal_arity` |

**`Date` has one member.** `new Date()`, `Date()`, `Date.parse`, `Date.UTC`,
any other member, and `Date` or `Date.now` used as a value are all refused under
one rule: `` `new Date()` is refused: Nish has no `Date` object; the one `Date`
member is `Date.now()`, the wall clock in milliseconds `` (NL2401;
`reject_os_date_new`, `reject_os_date_call`, `reject_os_date_parse`,
`reject_os_date_utc`, `reject_os_date_value`, `reject_os_date_bare`). A local
named `Date` shadows the global as any local does, so calling it is the
ordinary `` Unknown function `Date` `` (`reject_os_date_shadowed`). **`crypto`
has one member** the same way: `` `crypto.randomUUID` is refused: the one
`crypto` member is `crypto.getRandomValues(bytes)` `` (NL2403). The array
`getRandomValues` fills is written, so a `readonly u8[]` is refused as a store
through it is, a parameter it fills is never `readonly` in the IR, and inside a
scope's region it is refused on an array a task may read, as `fill` is. Anything
but a `u8[]` is `` `crypto.getRandomValues` fills a `u8[]`, got i32[] ``
(NL2402).

**A descriptor, not a handler.** A handler would be a function value, which the
language does not have, and would run between any two instructions of the
program. A descriptor is what a server's loop can wait on beside its sockets
(WP34 N5 will add that wait); until then `readSignal` is the blocking read.
Underneath it is a handler rather than a Linux `signalfd`, because a `signalfd`
hears only a signal blocked in every thread, and a mask reaches only the thread
that sets it. A child that `spawnSync` or `spawnSyncTo` starts after
`signalFd()` can still be stopped by either signal, because `exec` resets a
caught signal to its default (`os_signal`). Signals other than SIGTERM and
SIGINT are not in the language.

**On wasm.** A `wasm32` target and the `wasi` profile have no host for these to
reach, and `runtime-host.c` is empty there, so all five are refused by the
checker: `` `Date.now` reaches the operating system, and a wasm32 build has none
to reach `` (NL2404; `reject_os_now_wasm`, `reject_os_random_wasm`,
`reject_os_mtime_wasm`, `reject_os_signal_fd_wasm`, `reject_os_read_signal_wasm`).

**The TypeScript reading** ([wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §2).
`Date.now` is **class A**: Node's is the same floored `CLOCK_REALTIME`, and the
`os_` block of `tests/run.js` holds both readings between two reads of Node's
own clock. `statMtimeSync` is **class A** under `runtime/nish.mjs`, which answers
`fs.statSync(path, { throwIfNoEntry: false })?.mtimeMs`, or NaN: the `os_`
block sets a file's mtime to a fraction of a millisecond and requires the
native build and the prelude both to print Node's `mtimeMs` for it.
`crypto.getRandomValues` is **class A under the prelude** and class C without
it: Node's own takes only a typed array and a `u8[]` is a plain `Array` there,
so the prelude replaces the method on Node's `crypto` with one that fills a
plain array too and panics past 65,536 with the native words; `os_random` and
`os_random_limit` run unmodified under it. `signalFd` and `readSignal` are
**class C**, with no synchronous reading at all: Node delivers a signal only to
its event loop, which a blocking `readSignal` never returns to, so the prelude's
versions throw rather than answer. The row in
[wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §3.5 gives the translation.

## Children and the machine: `spawn`, `kill`, `waitPid`, `availableParallelism`, `totalMemory`

What a supervisor asks of the host (WP34 N12): start a child without waiting
for it, stop it, reap it when it ends, and size itself to the machine it runs
on. All five are C in `runtime/runtime-os.c`, beside `spawnSync`, and each is
exported by `nish:process` as well as being a global.

Reference: [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spawn(argv: string[]): i32` | start `argv[0]` exactly as `spawnSync` does and answer the child's **pid** at once, **without waiting**, or a **negative errno** (-22 for an empty vector or an argument holding a NUL). **Test `pid > 0` before handing the answer on**: a failure passed to `waitPid` reads as "any child". A child never reaped stays a zombie until the program exits | write | `os_spawn`; `reject_os_spawn_type`, `reject_os_spawn_wasm` |
| `spawnWithFds(argv: string[], fds: readonly i32[]): i32` | `spawn`, with the child holding `fds[i]` as descriptor **`3 + i`**, close-on-exec cleared there. **No other descriptor** of this process reaches it but one opened without close-on-exec, which nothing the runtime opens is. More than **64** descriptors, or a negative one, is `-22` before anything is opened or started. The child shares each descriptor's open file, offset and status flags, and this process keeps its own. Its pid, or a negative errno | write | `spawn_fds_child`, `caps_process_spawn_fds`; `reject_spawn_fds_arity`, `reject_spawn_fds_element`, `reject_spawn_fds_argv`, `reject_spawn_fds_wasm` |
| `kill(pid: i32, sig: i32): i32` | send `sig` to `pid` and answer 0, or a negative errno. **Only 0, 2 (SIGINT), 9 (SIGKILL) and 15 (SIGTERM)**, whose numbers are the same on Linux and Darwin; any other `sig` is -22, and so is a `pid` of 0 or below, which `kill(2)` reads as more than one process. A positive pid may be any process of this user, not only a child ([RT-19](../../security/runtime.md)) | write | `os_kill`; `reject_os_kill_f64`, `reject_os_kill_wasm` |
| `waitPid(pid: i32, flags: i32): i32[]` | reap a child (`pid` a child's or **-1 for any child**; flag **1 is WNOHANG**) and answer a fresh **`[pid, status]`**, the status as `spawnSync`'s; a failure puts the negative errno first. After `signalFd()` a blocking wait never sees EINTR, because that handler is installed with `SA_RESTART` and the wait restarts. An array because the language has no tuple | write | `os_wait`, `os_spawn`, `os_kill`; `reject_os_wait_arity`, `reject_os_wait_wasm` |
| `availableParallelism(): i32` | the CPUs this program may use, **at least 1**: the smallest of the CPUs online, its affinity mask or cpuset, a cgroup v2 CPU quota rounded up, and a positive `NISH_NUM_THREADS`, which can lower the count and never raise it. It needs no `--threads` | none | `os_cpu`; `reject_os_cpu_arity`, `reject_os_cpu_wasm` |
| `totalMemory(): i64` | bytes of **physical memory**, or **-1** where the host does not say. The machine's, not a cgroup's limit | none | `os_memory`; `reject_os_memory_wasm` |

**Capabilities.** `spawn`, `kill` and `waitPid` carry `process.spawn`, the
label `spawnSync` carries: each reaches other processes — `kill` any process of
this user, as kill(1) does, not only a child `spawn` started — so none takes a
label of its own (`caps_process_wait`).
`availableParallelism` and `totalMemory` carry **none**: how many cores and
bytes the machine has is a fact about the host, as `process.platform` is, read
to size a program rather than to reach anything (`caps_host`).

**In a task.** `spawn`, `kill` and `waitPid` write state outside the program,
so a scope's task or a parallel body that calls one — under any import alias —
is refused as any shared write is (`reject_os_spawn_task`,
`reject_os_kill_task`, `reject_os_wait_task`, `reject_os_kill_task_alias`,
`reject_os_kill_parallel`). `availableParallelism` and `totalMemory` write
nothing and may be called there (`tests/link/thread_host_facts_task`).

**On wasm.** A `wasm32` target has no processes and no host to ask, so all five
are refused by the checker with the N3 rule's words: `` `spawn` reaches the
operating system, and a wasm32 build has none to reach `` (NL2404;
`reject_os_spawn_wasm`, `reject_os_kill_wasm`, `reject_os_wait_wasm`,
`reject_os_cpu_wasm`, `reject_os_memory_wasm`).

**The TypeScript reading.** `kill`, `availableParallelism` and `totalMemory`
are **class A** under `runtime/nish.mjs`: `kill` checks the signal and the pid
as the native one does and turns Node's error code back into its errno;
`availableParallelism` is `os.availableParallelism()` lowered by
`NISH_NUM_THREADS` (Node reads no cgroup quota, so inside a container with one
the two can differ); and `totalMemory` is `os.totalmem()`, a `bigint` as every
`i64` is there. `spawn` and `waitPid` are **class C**: Node reaps its children
itself, on the event loop, so a synchronous wait has nothing to find, and the
prelude's versions throw, naming themselves, rather than answer (the `os_`
block of `tests/run.js`).

## Scheduling: `setNice`, `setIdlePriority`, `setCpuAffinity`

How much of the CPU the program asks for, and where: a batch job or a background indexer
steps aside for the interactive work on the machine, and a prefork worker keeps to one core. Each is C in
`runtime/runtime-os.c`, and each is exported by `nish:process` as well as
being a global.

Reference: [`nish:process`](../nish-process.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `setNice(n: i32): i32` | set the **nice value** with `setpriority(PRIO_PROCESS, 0, n)` and answer 0, or a negative errno. **Lower-only**, even as root: outside 0..19 is `-22` and below the current value is `-13`, both with no system call, so the priority never rises. Children started afterwards inherit it | write | `os_nice`; `reject_os_nice_wasm`, `reject_os_nice_task` |
| `setIdlePriority(): i32` | move the program to **`SCHED_IDLE`** with `sched_setscheduler(0, SCHED_IDLE, …)` and answer 0 or a negative errno. **Linux only**: Darwin answers -95 (Linux's EOPNOTSUPP, as `nish:net` spells it). **An unprivileged process can never leave `SCHED_IDLE`**, and an idle process can **starve** on a saturated machine, so a caller keeps a normal-priority fallback for work that must finish | write | `os_nice`; `reject_os_idle_wasm` |
| `setCpuAffinity(cpu: i32): i32` | pin the calling process to the one CPU `cpu` with `sched_setaffinity` and answer 0, or a negative errno. **Narrow-only**: a `cpu` outside the CPUs the process may already run on (`taskset`, a cgroup) is `-22` with no change. `availableParallelism()` answers 1 afterwards. **Linux only**: -95 on Darwin and under Node | write | `link/net_prefork_pin`; `reject_os_affinity_wasm`, `reject_os_affinity_task` |

**Per thread.** Linux keeps both the nice value and the policy per thread: a
call sets the calling thread's and every thread started after it. So both
belong at the top of `main`, before a `scope()` or a parallel loop starts the
pool, and a task or a parallel body that calls one is refused as any shared
write is (`reject_os_nice_task`). Neither ever crashes the program: a failure
is only the answer.

**Capabilities.** Both carry `process.spawn`, the label `kill` carries: neither
reaches another process, but the priority is the one the program's children
inherit, and a step down cannot always be taken back.

**On wasm.** A `wasm32` target schedules nothing of the host's, so both are
refused by the checker with the N3 rule's words (NL2404;
`reject_os_nice_wasm`, `reject_os_idle_wasm`).

**The TypeScript reading.** Both are **class C** under `runtime/nish.mjs`:
Node has `os.setPriority` but no `SCHED_IDLE`, and a reading of one without
the other would differ from the native build on the same host, so both throw,
naming themselves.

## `nish:net`: addresses, non-blocking TCP and UDP, and the readiness loop

Sockets for a program that owns its loop (WP34 N5): a server listens, accepts
and reads and writes bytes, a client connects, or either binds and trades
datagrams, and every socket is
**non-blocking**, so a call that
would wait answers "would block" instead, and the program decides what to do
next. There is no callback, and an [`async` function](declarations.md#async-functions-async-and-await)
cannot wait on a socket yet (its tasks run on an in-process queue): the program
is the loop, and it waits in [`pollWait`](#the-readiness-loop) for
whichever of its descriptors is ready. Every socket is also **close-on-exec**,
so a child that `spawnSync` starts inherits none of them. All twenty-six functions
are C in
`runtime/runtime-net.c`, a translation unit of its own with its own `.text*`
ceiling, which `scripts/build.sh` compiles beside `runtime.c` as it does the
others; section GC leaves every one of them out of a program that calls none
(the `net_` block of `tests/run.js` links one and counts the symbols). Each is
exported by `nish:net` and is a global too, as every `nish:` export is.

Reference: [`nish:net`](../nish-net.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `netAddress(out: u8[], host: string, port: i32): i32` | writes the [address form](#the-address-form) of a **numeric** host and `port` into `out`: `0`, or `-22`, leaving `out` as it was. No `nish:net` call looks a name up; [`nish/net/dns`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/std/net/dns.ts) resolves it first | write | `net_tcp_calls`, `net_tcp_import`; `reject_net_unknown_export` |
| `netLocalPort(fd: i32): i32` | the port the socket is bound to, the one the kernel chose for a listen on port `0` | write | `net_tcp_calls`, `net_tcp_echo` |
| `tcpListen(host: string, port: i32, backlog: i32): i32` | a listening socket on a numeric host with `SO_REUSEADDR`; `"::"` hears both families, and on a kernel without IPv6 it is IPv4's `0.0.0.0`. `-98` when the port is in use | write | `net_tcp_calls`, `net_tcp_echo`, `net_dual_stack`; `reject_net_arity`, `reject_net_wasm` |
| `tcpListenFlags(host: string, port: i32, backlog: i32, flags: i32): i32` | `tcpListen`'s socket, with flags: `1` `SO_REUSEPORT`, which differs by platform as the table below shows; `2` `TCP_NODELAY`, which the runtime sets on every accepted connection, on every platform, closing one on which it cannot; `4`, with `1`, steers each connection to the listener of the CPU that received it, Linux only (`-95` elsewhere, `-22` without `1`). Any other bit is `-22` before a socket is made | write | `net_tcp_reuseport`, `net_tcp_nodelay`, `link/net_tcp_reuseport_spread`, `link/net_tcp_nodelay_shared`; `reject_net_reuseport_wasm`, `reject_net_nodelay_wasm` |
| `tcpAccept(fd: i32, peer: u8[]): i32` | the next waiting connection, non-blocking and close-on-exec, with the peer's address in `peer`; `-11` when none is waiting, and a `peer` shorter than 18 bytes is `-22` before a connection is taken. Not `willreturn`: on a blocking socket the program inherited it waits | write | `net_tcp_calls`, `net_tcp_echo`; `reject_net_accept_readonly` |
| `netRead(fd: i32, buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | at most `len` bytes into `buf[off, off + len)`: the count, `0` at the end of the stream, or `-11` when nothing is waiting. The range is [checked](#bounds) | write | `net_tcp_echo`, `net_tcp_bounds`; `reject_net_readonly`, `reject_net_element`, `reject_net_import_wasm` |
| `netWrite(fd: i32, buf: readonly u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | at most `len` bytes of `buf[off, off + len)`: the count, which may be short. A peer that has gone is **`-32`, never SIGPIPE**, so a closed connection cannot end the process. The range is [checked](#bounds) | write | `net_tcp_echo`, `net_tcp_bounds`; `reject_net_write_element` |
| `netWrite2(fd: i32, a: readonly u8[], aOff: i32, aLen: i32, b: readonly u8[], bOff: i32, bLen: i32): i32` | two ranges in **one system call** (`sendmsg` with two `iovec`s), answered as `netWrite` is, `-32` and never SIGPIPE included. Both ranges are [checked](#bounds), `a`'s first. As for every call here, a `wasm32` build refuses it and Node throws | write | `tests/link/net_write2`, `net_write2_bounds`; `reject_net_write2_element`, `reject_net_write2_element_a`, `reject_net_write2_wasm` |
| `netShutdown(fd: i32, how: i32): i32` | shuts the read side (`0`), the write side (`1`) or both (`2`) | write | `net_tcp_calls` |
| `netClose(fd: i32): i32` | closes the descriptor, which is gone after the call whatever the answer. Not `willreturn`, because a socket the program inherited with a linger time can wait | write | `net_tcp_calls`, `net_tcp_echo`; `reject_net_fd_type` |
| `netSetOption(fd: i32, option: i32, value: i32): i32` | sets one [socket option](#socket-options) from a whitelist; any other `option` is **`-22`**, so there is no way to pass a raw level and name through. `NET_TCP_QUICKACK` is Linux's, **`-95` elsewhere** | write | `net_set_option`; `reject_net_set_option_wasm` |
| `netMss(fd: i32): i32` | the maximum segment size a connected TCP socket sends, or **a plain `-1`, never an errno,** for every other descriptor and every call on wasm. It never panics | write | `net_mss`; `reject_net_mss_arity`, `reject_net_mss_type`; `net_mss` in `tests/run.js` for wasm32 and WASI |
| `unixListen(path: string, backlog: i32, flags: i32): i32` | a listening [Unix-domain](#unix-domain-sockets) stream socket at `path`, whose file only its owner may connect to (`0600`); its paths and refusals are under that heading | write | `net_unix_calls`, `net_unix_paths`, `net_unix_fds`; `reject_net_unix_arity`, `reject_net_unix_wasm` |
| `unixListenMode(path: string, backlog: i32, flags: i32, mode: i32): i32` | `unixListen`'s socket with the file's mode chosen, `0` to `0o777`, set before the listen so no connect gets in under a wider one; an abstract name is `-22` | write | `net_unix_paths`, `net_unix_calls` |
| `unixConnect(path: string): i32` | a new socket, non-blocking and close-on-exec, connected to the listener at `path`; a full backlog is `-11` on Linux and `-111` on Darwin | write | `net_unix_calls`, `net_unix_paths`; `reject_net_unix_path_type` |
| `unixAccept(fd: i32): i32` | the next waiting connection, non-blocking and close-on-exec; no peer address is written | write | `net_unix_calls` |
| `unixSocketPair(kind: i32, fds: i32[]): i32` | two connected sockets into `fds`, non-blocking and close-on-exec, of kind `1` (`NET_UNIX_STREAM`) or `2` (`NET_UNIX_SEQPACKET`). Kind `2` is **`-95` on Darwin** | write | `net_unix_calls`, `net_unix_fds`; `reject_net_unix_pair_element`, `reject_net_unix_pair_readonly` |
| `sendFd(sock: i32, fd: i32, buf: readonly u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | bytes over the Unix socket `sock` with one copy of `fd` riding on them (`SCM_RIGHTS`). A `len` of `0` is **`-22`**, a socket of another family **`-95`**, and a gone peer `-32`, never SIGPIPE. The range is [checked](#bounds) | write | `net_unix_scm`, `net_unix_scm_bounds`; `reject_net_unix_scm_arity`, `reject_net_unix_scm_wasm` |
| `recvFd(sock: i32, buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32, fd: i32[]): i32` | bytes from the Unix socket `sock`, with the first descriptor the message carried in `fd[0]`, or **`-1`**; every further one is closed before the answer. The one kept is close-on-exec and **not** made non-blocking. The range is [checked](#bounds) | write | `net_unix_scm`, `net_unix_scm_bounds`; `reject_net_unix_scm_element`, `reject_net_unix_scm_readonly`, `reject_net_unix_scm_buf_readonly`, `reject_net_unix_scm_wasm` |
| `peerCredentials(fd: i32, out: i32[]): i32` | the pid, uid and gid of the process at the other end of a connected Unix socket, as the kernel recorded them **when the connection was made**, not who holds the other end now. A socket with no peer is **`-107`** on every platform; on Darwin the pid is `-1` where the SDK has no `LOCAL_PEERPID` or the kernel refuses it | write | `net_unix_scm`, `caps_net_peer`; `reject_net_unix_peer_arity`, `reject_net_unix_peer_readonly`, `reject_net_unix_peer_element`, `reject_net_unix_scm_wasm` |

What `tcpListenFlags`'s flag `1` does on each platform:

| Platform | Flag `1` |
| --- | --- |
| Linux | Listeners that share the port each get new connections, spread by a hash of the connection's 4-tuple; only listeners of the same user may share |
| Darwin | Listeners share the port, but one of them takes the connections: the flag buys a restart without a gap rather than a spread; flag `4` is `-95` |
| `wasm32`, `--profile wasi` | Refused at compile time with NL2404, as every `nish:net` call is |

**Errors are numbers.** Every call answers an `i32`: `>= 0` is success (a
descriptor, a count, `0`), and a negative number is the failure's errno,
negated. The codes a loop branches on are **Linux's numbers on every platform**:
`-11` would block, `-95` unsupported, `-32` the peer has gone, `-104` the
connection was reset, `-98` the address is in use, `-111` the connection was
refused, `-110` it timed out, `-88` not a socket and `-22` a bad argument; the Darwin runtime
translates its own. Any other failure is the host's `-errno`
(`-9` for a descriptor that is not open, on both). `-95` is what `tcpAccept`
answers for a datagram socket, on both (`net_udp_calls`). A number rather than a
`Result`, because no builtin answers one and a failure here is routine, and
because a number allocates nothing. It follows the shape `signalFd` set, where
a negative `i32` is a failure, and adds the errno to it: `signalFd` and
`readSignal` answer a plain `-1` for any failure (and `readFileBytesSync`
answers `null`), while a `nish:net` call says which failure it was, so a loop
tells "would block" from "the peer has gone" without asking again. No
`nish:net` call touches the arena (`net_tcp_echo` serves two hundred messages
in a loop whose pass scope gives back what each pass builds, and prints `flat`
when that moved the arena no further than one message did).

### Socket options

`netSetOption`'s `option` is one of five ids `nish:net` exports, each an `i32`
and each a global too. They are the runtime's own numbers, not the kernel's,
so a program reads the same on Linux and Darwin, and the runtime maps each to
its level and name; there is no raw passthrough, because a level, a name and a
length the program spells is an untyped call into the kernel.

| Id | Value | Sets | `value` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `NET_TCP_NODELAY` | `1` | `IPPROTO_TCP`, `TCP_NODELAY` | `1` sends a small write at once, `0` lets Nagle's algorithm batch it |
| `NET_TCP_QUICKACK` | `2` | `IPPROTO_TCP`, `TCP_QUICKACK`, Linux only; **`-95` on Darwin** | `1` acknowledges at once, `0` lets the kernel delay the ACK. Linux does not keep the mode: it leaves it on its own, so a server that wants one sets it again after every response |
| `NET_SO_KEEPALIVE` | `3` | `SOL_SOCKET`, `SO_KEEPALIVE` | `1` probes an idle connection |
| `NET_SO_SNDBUF` | `4` | `SOL_SOCKET`, `SO_SNDBUF` | bytes; Linux doubles the value it stores |
| `NET_SO_RCVBUF` | `5` | `SOL_SOCKET`, `SO_RCVBUF` | bytes; Linux doubles the value it stores |

An id is read as a value, as `platform` is: it folds to its number in the IR,
cannot be assigned, and is not a [module constant](declarations.md#module-constants), so a
module constant cannot be initialised from one. A local of the same name
shadows the global spelling.

`netMss`'s `-1` is one answer, not an errno, because a program does the same
thing for every reason there is no MSS: it uses a size of its own. That is also
why it compiles on wasm when `netSetOption` is refused there: a socket option a
program sets is an effect a wasm build cannot have, while a size it reads has
an honest answer everywhere, "none".

### The address form

An address is **18 bytes of a `u8[]`**: the 16 bytes of an IPv6 address, with
an IPv4 address written as the mapped `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, then the port,
big-endian, so `127.0.0.1:8080` is ten zeros, `255 255`, `127 0 0 1`, `31 144`
(`net_tcp_calls`). One form for both families, in memory the caller owns, so a
server that accepts a million connections allocates nothing to learn who they
are from.

**Both families on one socket.** `net_dual_stack` listens on `"::"`, and the
`net_` block of `tests/run.js` connects to it from Node over `127.0.0.1` and
then over `::1`: the first peer arrives as `::ffff:127.0.0.1` and the second as
`::1`, each with Node's own port in the last two bytes, and both are echoed.
Its UDP socket, bound to `"::"` too, sends itself a datagram with each ECN mark
to its IPv4 address and to its IPv6 one, and reads every mark back from
`meta[1]` over both. That needs a host with IPv6: where `::1` cannot be listened
on, `"::"` is the IPv4 fallback above, and the check says so and passes rather
than counting a skip. CI's `ubuntu-latest` has IPv6 and runs it.

### The client half

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tcpConnect(addr: readonly u8[]): i32` | a new TCP socket, non-blocking and close-on-exec, that starts connecting to the [address](#the-address-form) in `addr` and answers its descriptor **at once, while the connection is still being made**; the loop reports it writable when that has finished. Any other failure closes the socket and is answered instead of it | write | `net_tcp_connect`, `net_tcp_connect_import`; `reject_net_connect_element`, `reject_net_connect_arity` |
| `connectResult(fd: i32): i32` | how the connection went, asked once `fd` is writable: `0`, or its failure from `SO_ERROR`, such as **`-111` for a port nobody listens on**. The kernel clears the failure as it is read | write | `net_tcp_connect`, `net_tcp_connect_import`; `reject_net_connect_wasm` |

A connection is made the way everything else here waits: in the loop. Linux
answers `EINPROGRESS` even over loopback, so a program asks for writability and
not for an answer from the call. Neither call waits, so both are `willreturn`,
and neither allocates. `net_tcp_connect` is a Nish client and a Nish server in
one loop: two exchanges of 1 and 200 messages come back byte for byte with the
arena where it stood, and a port that was bound and closed again answers `-111`
and then `0`. The `net_` block of `tests/run.js` runs it under a timeout, so a
lost wake fails the run rather than hangs it.

```ts
const addr: u8[] = new Array<u8>(18);
netAddress(addr, "127.0.0.1", 8080);
const fd = tcpConnect(addr);          // the descriptor, still connecting
pollAdd(loop, fd, 2, 1);              // writable once it has finished
// ... pollWait until token 1 comes back ...
if (connectResult(fd) === 0) {
  pollModify(loop, fd, 1, 1);         // connected: now wait to read
}
```

### UDP

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `udpBind(host: string, port: i32, flags: i32): i32` | a datagram socket, non-blocking and close-on-exec, bound as `tcpListen`'s is, `"::"` and its IPv4 fallback included. Flag `1` is `SO_REUSEPORT`, flag `2` is `UDP_GRO`, and any other bit is `-22` | write | `net_udp_calls`, `net_udp_echo`, `net_udp_offload`, `net_dual_stack`; `reject_net_udp_wasm`, `reject_net_udp_parallel` |
| `udpSendTo(fd: i32, buf: readonly u8[], off: i32, len: i32, to: readonly u8[], segment: i32, ecn: i32): i32` | `buf[off, off + len)` to `to` in one `sendmsg`, cut by the kernel into datagrams of `segment` bytes when that is above `0` (**GSO**), with `ecn` as the IP header's two ECN bits. Not `willreturn`: on a blocking socket the program inherited it waits. The range is [checked](#bounds) | write | `net_udp_calls`, `net_udp_echo`, `net_udp_offload`, `net_udp_bounds`; `reject_net_udp_send_element`, `reject_net_udp_arity`, `reject_net_udp_task` |
| `udpRecvFrom(fd: i32, buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32, from: u8[], meta: i32[]): i32` | the next datagram into `buf[off, off + len)`, cut to `len`, in one `recvmsg`, with its sender in `from`, its **GRO** segment size in `meta[0]` and its ECN bits in `meta[1]`; `-11` when none is waiting. Not `willreturn`, as `udpSendTo`. The range is [checked](#bounds) | write | `net_udp_calls`, `net_udp_echo`, `net_udp_offload`, `net_udp_bounds`; `reject_net_udp_readonly`, `reject_net_udp_meta_readonly`, `reject_net_udp_meta_element`, `reject_net_udp_element`, `reject_net_udp_region` |

A datagram carries no stream, so an echo is `udpRecvFrom` and then `udpSendTo`
back to `from`, which is already an address; the `net_` block of
`tests/run.js` drives `net_udp_echo` from Node's `dgram`, two hundred
datagrams in a round, and requires every byte back and the arena flat. An
empty datagram is a datagram: `udpRecvFrom` answers `0` for it, which is how
`net_udp_echo` ends a round. A socket that is IPv4 — bound to an IPv4 host, or
to `"::"` on a kernel without IPv6 — sends to a mapped `::ffff:a.b.c.d`
address as IPv4 (`net_udp_calls`).

**Segmentation offload.** On Linux, one `udpSendTo` of 4,800 bytes with
`segment = 1200` leaves as four datagrams of 1,200, which a Node `dgram` socket
receives one by one. A socket bound with flag `2` receives what one such send
left as **one** datagram of up to 64 KB with `meta[0] == 1200`, while a socket
without it receives the four apart, each with `meta[0] == 0`
(`net_udp_offload`, run by the `net_` block). The kernel coalesces only
datagrams of one flow, and only those that arrive after the option is set,
which is why it is a flag of `udpBind`; on loopback it coalesces what left as
one GSO send, not datagrams sent one by one. The ECN bits a send asks for
arrive in the receiver's `meta[1]` (`net_udp_offload`). Measured on loopback,
Nish sender to Nish receiver, 1,200-byte datagrams: 459,000 a second at one
per call, and 1,760,000 a second sent with `segment = 1200` over 49,200-byte
sends.

**Darwin has none of the three.** There `udpSendTo` with a `segment` or an
`ecn` above `0`, and `udpBind` with flag `2`, answer `-95`, and `meta` is
always `0, 0`. A `meta[1]` of `0` is also what a datagram that really is not
ECN-capable reads as, so a receive on Darwin cannot say ECN is unsupported: a
program learns that from the `-95` a send with an `ecn` above `0` answers, and
on Darwin it reads every arrival as Not-ECT. CI's `runtime-net` (macos-latest)
job runs that branch: the `net_` sections there take the `-95` a GSO send and a
GRO bind answer, and fall back to one datagram a send (`net_loopback`,
`net_relay`), and `net_udp_offload` requires the `-95` of GSO, the GRO bind and
each ECN mark, with nothing sent by them while a plain send still arrives. On Linux no UDP call answers `-95`, and the code is pinned there
by `tcpAccept` on a datagram socket instead, above.

### The readiness loop

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pollCreate(): i32` | a loop: a descriptor, close-on-exec, that watches others — epoll on Linux, kqueue on Darwin | write | `net_loop_calls`, `net_loop_two`; `reject_net_poll_wasm` |
| `pollAdd(loop: i32, fd: i32, events: i32, token: i32): i32` | watches `fd` for `events` (`1` readable, `2` writable) and reports it under `token`, an `i32` of the program's choosing; `-17` for a descriptor the loop already watches | write | `net_loop_calls`, `net_loop_two`; `reject_net_poll_arity`, `reject_net_poll_parallel` |
| `pollModify(loop: i32, fd: i32, events: i32, token: i32): i32` | new events or a new token for a watched descriptor; `-2` for one the loop does not watch | write | `net_loop_calls`, `net_loop_two` |
| `pollRemove(loop: i32, fd: i32): i32` | stops watching `fd`; `-2` for one the loop does not watch. Closing a descriptor stops the watching too | write | `net_loop_calls`, `net_loop_two` |
| `pollWait(loop: i32, ready: i32[], timeoutMs: i32): i32` | waits until a watched descriptor is ready or `timeoutMs` passes, **forever for a negative one**, and writes a token and events pair per ready descriptor into `ready`, **`4` added for a hang-up or an error**: the count, at most 64, or **`0` on a timeout**. Not `willreturn`, because it can wait forever | write | `net_loop_calls`, `net_loop_two`; `reject_net_poll_readonly`, `reject_net_poll_element`, `reject_net_poll_task`, `reject_net_poll_region` |

**Level-triggered.** A descriptor that is still ready when the program waits
again is reported again, so a loop that handles one pair of several, or leaves
a datagram unread, loses nothing: `net_loop_calls` sends a datagram and waits
twice, and both waits report it. The same is why the 64 a call reports at most
is a bound on a stack array rather than on the program: the rest are still
ready at the next wait. A UDP socket is always writable, and on Linux one whose
both sides are shut is readable, writable and hung up, `7` (`net_loop_calls`).
Nothing allocates; `ready` is the caller's.

**A signal wakes the loop.** The descriptor `signalFd()` answers is a
descriptor like any other, readable when SIGTERM or SIGINT arrives, so a server
adds it to its loop and shuts down when its token comes back: `readSignal`
then answers the number without waiting. A signal that interrupts the wait
itself makes `pollWait` answer **`0`**, as a timeout does, rather than wait on
past the deadline it was given; the loop comes round and the next wait finds
the signal descriptor ready (`tests/runtime-test.c`). `net_loop_two` watches
two UDP sockets and `signalFd()` in one loop, and the `net_` block of
`tests/run.js` drives it from Node: it writes to one socket and waits for the
line that says that socket woke the loop before it writes to the other, in both
orders, and then sends SIGTERM, which wakes the loop through the signal
descriptor; the program reads `15`, prints `flat` because the arena stood
where it did at the top of every pass, and exits `0`.

```ts
const loop = pollCreate();
pollAdd(loop, server, 1, 1);
pollAdd(loop, signalFd(), 1, 2);
const ready: i32[] = new Array<i32>(32);
let running = true;
while (running) {
  const n = pollWait(loop, ready, -1);
  for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) {
    if (ready[2 * k] === 2) {
      running = false;             // SIGTERM or SIGINT
    } else {
      serve(server);               // until it answers -11
    }
  }
}
```

**Darwin** is kqueue, with a filter per direction rather than a set of events,
and the runtime builds epoll's answers from the filters: `pollAdd` of a
descriptor already watched is `-17`, `pollModify` and `pollRemove` of one not
watched are `-2`, a descriptor added watching nothing holds a disabled read
filter so the loop still knows it, and a descriptor both readable and writable
is one pair, `3`, folded from its two filters' records. Three differences
stay. The `pollAdd` that answers `-17` leaves the descriptor, both ways, under
the token it gave rather than the old one. A descriptor watching nothing is
never reported: epoll still reports its hang-up or error as `4`, but a disabled
filter reports nothing. And a peer's half-close is `1` on Linux but `5`, `1|4`,
on Darwin: kqueue marks the read filter with end-of-file as soon as the FIN
arrives, and the runtime reads end-of-file as `4`, where epoll sets its
hang-up bit only once both directions are shut. CI's
`runtime-net` (macos-latest) job runs `net_loop_calls` and `net_loop_two` on a
mac, as it runs every `net_` section.

### Unix-domain sockets

A Unix-domain socket is named by a path rather than a host and port, and
reaches only processes on the same machine. Once made, it is a descriptor like
any other: `netRead`, `netWrite`, `netShutdown`, `netClose` and the readiness
loop take it as they take a TCP one, and a peer that has gone is `-32` here
too. There is no address form: `unixAccept` writes no peer.

- **The path.** It is bytes up to the first NUL, so a NUL inside it is `-22`,
  as an empty path is. It must fit `sun_path` with its NUL: **107 bytes on
  Linux, 103 on Darwin**, and a longer one is `-36` before a socket exists,
  rather than the kernel's cut-short name binding a file the program never
  named. A relative path is the working directory's, and the limit is on the
  string as written, not the absolute path it resolves to.
- **Abstract names.** A path that starts with `@` is Linux's abstract
  namespace: the rest, at most 107 bytes, is the name, nothing is made on the
  file system and nothing is left behind when the socket closes. A bare `@` is
  `-22`. Darwin has none, and there every `@` path is **`-95`**. A file whose
  name starts with `@` is spelled `./@name`, which is a relative path like any
  other.
- **The file's mode.** A pathname listener's file is `0600` for `unixListen`,
  so only its owner may connect, and `unixListenMode`'s `mode` otherwise. The
  runtime sets it between the bind and the listen, while every connect is
  still refused, so the umask's mode is never one a client gets in under. A
  connect needs write permission on the file, and search permission on every
  directory above it, which is the real boundary: put the socket in a
  directory only the users who may connect can reach.
- **A path that exists.** A bind never replaces a file. A path that exists is
  `-98`, whatever is there, and flag `1`, `NET_UNIX_UNLINK_STALE`, clears only
  a socket file nothing listens on, the one a server that died left: the
  runtime connects to it, and only a refusal makes it unlink the file and bind
  again. On Linux a live listener, even one whose backlog is full, stays
  `-98`; a regular file, a directory or a link is `-17` and left alone. On
  Darwin a connect to a listener whose backlog is full is refused just as one
  to a dead file is, so the probe cannot tell them apart: there a socket file
  in the way is **`-95`** and left alone, and the flag never unlinks one;
  remove a file the program knows is its own with `unlinkSync`. The probe is
  a connection the live listener sees close at once. Between the probe and the
  unlink another process can bind the path, which is why the directory must
  be the program's own ([docs/security/runtime.md](../../security/runtime.md),
  RT-34).
- **Cleanup.** Closing a listener does **not** unlink its file: `unlinkSync`
  it when the server stops, or let the next start's flag `1` clear it. A
  `unixListen` that fails after its bind closes the socket and unlinks the
  file it made, so no failure leaves a descriptor or a file behind
  (`net_unix_fds` counts the descriptors around every failure, a chmod made
  to fail after the bind among them, and checks that none of the paths it
  named is left on disk).
- **Pairs.** `unixSocketPair` makes two sockets already connected to each
  other. `NET_UNIX_STREAM` is a byte stream, as a connection is;
  `NET_UNIX_SEQPACKET` keeps each write one message, so a read returns one
  message, never two run together (`net_unix_calls`). Darwin has no Unix
  seqpacket, and kind `2` there is `-95`.
- **Descriptors and credentials.** The descriptor `recvFd` gets for one
  `sendFd` sent is a new descriptor for the same open file, with its offset and
  status flags shared, as `dup` gives. `recvFd` keeps the
  first descriptor of a message and closes every other one before it answers,
  so a peer cannot leave this process holding descriptors it never asked for
  ([docs/security/runtime.md](../../security/runtime.md), RT-37). The one it keeps
  is close-on-exec, so a later `spawn` does not hand it on, but it is not made
  non-blocking: `netRead` on a blocking one waits, so set what the program
  needs on it before it joins a loop. `peerCredentials` names the process at
  the other end as the kernel recorded it at the connect; a peer that has
  changed its uid since, or passed the socket on, still reads as it was then
  (RT-39). On a TCP socket, or any socket not `AF_UNIX`, the three are
  `-95`, and on a descriptor that is not a socket `-88`, both before anything
  is sent or asked (`net_unix_scm`).

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NET_UNIX_UNLINK_STALE` | `1` | `unixListen`'s flag: clear a socket file nothing listens on |
| `NET_UNIX_STREAM` | `1` | `unixSocketPair`'s byte-stream kind |
| `NET_UNIX_SEQPACKET` | `2` | `unixSocketPair`'s message kind; `-95` on Darwin |

`NET_UNIX_UNLINK_STALE` and `NET_UNIX_STREAM` are both `1`, as
`NET_TCP_NODELAY` is: the constants are plain `i32`s, so the checker cannot
tell one passed where another belongs. Name the one the call takes.

On Darwin the calls are the same C under `#if`, with seven differences: no
abstract names (`-95`), no seqpacket pair (`-95`), flag `1` meeting a socket
file is `-95` rather than a probe, a connect to a full backlog is `-111`
rather than `-11`, `fcntl` after `accept` and `socketpair` where Linux
passes `SOCK_NONBLOCK | SOCK_CLOEXEC`, `fcntl` after `recvmsg` where Linux
passes `MSG_CMSG_CLOEXEC`, so a child another thread spawns between the two
inherits the descriptor `recvFd` keeps (RT-38), and `peerCredentials` reading
`getpeereid` and `LOCAL_PEERPID`, its pid `-1` where that refuses, where
Linux reads `SO_PEERCRED`. A listener has no peer: Linux answers its own
process's credentials there, and what Darwin answers is not yet seen on a
mac. CI does not run them on a mac yet.

### Bounds

`netRead`, `netWrite`, `netWrite2` (each of its two ranges), `udpSendTo` and `udpRecvFrom` check `0 <= off <= off +
len <= buf.length` **in the compiled code**, before the call, the way `dst.set(src, at)` checks the range it
writes, and a range outside it panics with the same words, `slice out of range:
[4, 9) of length 8`, exit 1 (`net_tcp_bounds`, `net_udp_bounds`, `net_write2_bounds`). A negative
`off` or `len` fails it. A `peer`, `out`, `to` or `from`
array shorter than 18 bytes, or a `meta` shorter than 2, is not a panic but
`-22`, from the runtime, because the length is the argument's
property rather than the program's arithmetic. So is a `ready` shorter than 2,
and `pollWait` never writes past `ready.length`, so it has no range to check.

### Types, threads and wasm

- **Bytes only.** Each buffer is a `u8[]`, as `crypto.getRandomValues`'s is: a
  socket carries bytes, and a wider element would make the byte order on the
  wire a fact about the machine. Anything else is `` `netRead` fills a `u8[]`,
  got i32[] `` (NL2402; `reject_net_element`) for a buffer the call writes, and
  `` `netWrite` sends from a `u8[]`, got string `` (NL2405;
  `reject_net_write_element`, `reject_net_udp_send_element`) for the one it
  reads. `udpRecvFrom`'s `meta` holds numbers rather than bytes, a segment size
  up to 65,535 among them, so it is an `i32[]`, and anything else is
  `` `udpRecvFrom` fills an `i32[]`, got u8[] `` (NL2406;
  `reject_net_udp_meta_element`), and so is `pollWait`'s `ready`, whose tokens
  are the program's own `i32`s (`` `pollWait` fills an `i32[]`, got u8[] ``,
  `reject_net_poll_element`), and so is `unixSocketPair`'s `fds`
  (`` `unixSocketPair` fills an `i32[]`, got u8[] ``,
  `reject_net_unix_pair_element`), and so are `recvFd`'s `fd` and
  `peerCredentials`'s `out` (`reject_net_unix_scm_element`,
  `reject_net_unix_peer_element`). A path is a `string`, and anything else is
  refused (`reject_net_unix_path_type`). A descriptor, an offset, a length, a port, a
  backlog, `how`, the flags, a segment size, the ECN bits, a loop, the events,
  a token, a timeout, a socket option and its value, a pair kind and a mode are `i32` in both number modes, and an
  `f64` is refused rather than converted (`reject_net_fd_type`).
- **What is written.** `netAddress`'s `out`, `tcpAccept`'s `peer`,
  `netRead`'s `buf`, `udpRecvFrom`'s `buf`, `from` and `meta`, `pollWait`'s
  `ready`, `unixSocketPair`'s `fds`, `recvFd`'s `buf` and `fd` and
  `peerCredentials`'s `out` are written, so
  a `readonly` array there is refused as a store through it is
  (`reject_net_readonly`, `reject_net_accept_readonly`,
  `reject_net_udp_readonly`, `reject_net_udp_meta_readonly`,
  `reject_net_poll_readonly`, `reject_net_unix_pair_readonly`,
  `reject_net_unix_scm_readonly`, `reject_net_unix_scm_buf_readonly`,
  `reject_net_unix_peer_readonly`), a parameter one of
  them fills is never `readonly` in the IR, and `netWrite`'s `buf`,
  `netWrite2`'s `a` and `b`, `udpSendTo`'s `buf` and `to` and `sendFd`'s `buf` may be `readonly` (`net_udp_calls`, `net_write2_bounds`).
- **Threads.** Every call changes the kernel's state of a socket, which is a
  write its caller can see, and a loop is a socket's state as much as its
  bytes, so none may be made in a `scope()` task
  (`reject_net_task`, `reject_net_udp_task`, `reject_net_poll_task`) or a
  parallel body (`reject_net_parallel`, `reject_net_udp_parallel`,
  `reject_net_poll_parallel`), and a call that writes an array is refused in a
  scope's region on one a task may read, as `fill` is (`reject_net_region`,
  `reject_net_udp_region` for `meta` and `reject_net_poll_region` for
  `ready`).
- **On wasm.** A `wasm32` target and the `wasi` profile have no sockets for these
  to reach, and `runtime-net.c` is empty there, so every call is refused by the
  checker with the host builtins' words: `` `tcpListen` reaches the operating
  system, and a wasm32 build has none to reach `` (NL2404; `reject_net_wasm`,
  `reject_net_import_wasm`, `reject_net_udp_wasm`, `reject_net_poll_wasm`,
  `reject_net_reuseport_wasm`, `reject_net_set_option_wasm`,
  `reject_net_unix_wasm`). The freestanding `--profile wasm` link, which
  takes IR compiled for the host, has no `runtime-net.c` either, so a program
  that calls one fails there at the link, on the undefined `nish_` symbol.
  The one exception is `netMss`, which compiles under a `wasm32` target and
  the `wasi` profile to the constant `-1`, its descriptor still evaluated,
  with no runtime call (`net_mss` in `tests/run.js`).
- **Not yet.** No `nish:net` call resolves a name (`reject_net_unknown_export`):
  the stub resolver is the library module `nish/net/dns`, which drives these
  calls on the program's own loop. There is no
  `sendmmsg` or `recvmmsg`, no edge-triggered mode and no timer
  but `pollWait`'s timeout. A program that does not want a loop can still wait
  for a connection, a byte or a datagram by calling again on `-11`, as
  `net_tcp_echo` and `net_udp_echo` do.

**The TypeScript reading** ([wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §2) is
**class C**, as `signalFd`'s is: Node's sockets are asynchronous only, and a
socket becomes ready only to Node's event loop, which a program that owns its
loop never returns to. `runtime/nish.d.ts` declares `nish:net` and the globals,
so `npm run check` types these programs, and under `runtime/nish.mjs` each
function throws `` `netAddress` has no synchronous reading under Node: a socket
is ready only to the event loop, which a program that owns its loop never
returns to (docs/wp33-round-trip.md) `` rather than answer `-11` forever (the
`net_` block of `tests/run.js`, for `netAddress`, `tcpConnect`, `udpBind` and
`pollCreate`). The option ids are plain numbers, so they read the same
under Node as natively, and `netSetOption` throws rather than set one
(`net_set_option` in `tests/run.js`). `netMss` throws too rather than answer `-1`: Node's
`net.Socket` has no MSS to read, and a `-1` would be a guess that the program
keeps (`net_mss` in `tests/run.js`). The same holds for the Unix-domain calls: the
`NET_UNIX_` constants read natively, and each of the five calls throws
(`net_unix` in `tests/run.js`). In a browser there are no sockets at all.
A loop has no reading either: the one a Node program has is Node's own, which
it returns to between callbacks, and `pollWait` is a program that never
returns to it.

## `nish:term`: terminal input

What a program needs to run a full-screen terminal interface: read a key the
moment it is pressed, wait for one with a timeout that doubles as a frame
clock, and ask the terminal whether it is one, how big it is, and to stop
echoing and line-editing. None of it needs the `net` capability that a
`pollAdd(0)` and `netRead(0, …)` would carry; the six functions carry
[`tty`](#capabilities) instead. They are C in `runtime/runtime-term.c`, a
translation unit of its own with its own `.text*` ceiling, which section GC
leaves out of a program that calls none of them. Each is exported by
`nish:term` and is a global too, as every `nish:` export is. Linux and Darwin
only, and WASI as below.

Reference: [`nish:term`](../nish-term.md).

| Signature | Semantics | Effect | Test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `readStdin(buf: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): i32` | at most `len` bytes of stdin into `buf[off, off + len)`, **without waiting**: the count, `0` at the end of the stream, or `-11` when nothing is waiting. The range is [checked](#bounds), and the buffer is a writable `u8[]` | write | `term_calls`, `term_import`; `reject_term_read_arity`, `reject_term_read_i32_buffer`, `reject_term_read_readonly` |
| `waitStdin(timeoutMs: i32): boolean` | waits until stdin is readable, its end and an error included, or `timeoutMs` passes, for ever for a negative one; `false` when the time ran out or a signal ended the wait early, but not for a Ctrl-Z and `fg` once `setRawMode(true)` has caught SIGTSTP, after which the wait goes on for what is left. Before raw mode Linux goes on with what is left and Darwin ends the wait. Not `willreturn` | write | `term_calls`, `term_import`, `term_pty`; `reject_term_wait_string` |
| `isTerminal(fd: i32): boolean` | whether the descriptor is a terminal (`isatty`) | write | `term_calls`, `term_pty`; `reject_term_is_terminal_arity` |
| `terminalSize(): i32[]` | a fresh `[columns, rows]` of the terminal on stdout, or on stderr when stdout is not one; **`[-25, 0]` for "not a terminal"** | write | `term_calls`, `term_pty`, `mem_terminal_size_scope`; `reject_term_size_arity` |
| `setRawMode(on: boolean): i32` | puts stdin's terminal in raw mode (`true`) or back as it was (`false`): `0`, or `-25` when stdin is not a terminal. `setRawMode(false)` is always safe | write | `term_calls`, `term_pty`; `reject_term_raw_number`, `reject_term_unknown_export` |
| `setTerminalRestore(bytes: string): i32` | keeps a copy of `bytes` for the runtime to write to the terminal on stdout as the program ends, **replacing** what it kept before: `0`, `-25` when stdout is not a terminal and `-7` (E2BIG) past `NISH_TERM_RESTORE_MAX`, 4096 bytes, both keeping what was there. When they go out is under [Raw mode](#raw-mode) | write | `term_restore`; `reject_term_restore_arity`, `reject_term_restore_number`, `reject_term_restore_wasm` |

**Errors are numbers**, in `nish:net`'s shape: `>= 0` is success and a negative
number the failure's errno, negated. The two a program branches on are the
same number on every platform: `-11`, nothing is waiting, and `-25`, not a
terminal. Any other is the host's own.

**stdin is never made non-blocking.** `O_NONBLOCK` belongs to the open file
description, which a shell shares with every program it starts, so a program
that set it and then crashed would leave the shell's own stdin non-blocking.
`readStdin` asks `select` with a timeout of `0` before it reads instead, and so
does `waitStdin`: Darwin's `poll` does not support devices, and answers a
terminal at once whether a key is waiting or not.

**The loop.** `waitStdin` is the frame clock: a game waits up to one frame for a
key, reads what came, advances the world and draws, so the wait costs nothing
