  data does (`tests/link/std_json_typed`, whose `main.ll` is the golden of the
  code written for a one-field class and `tag.ll` of the code for a `u64`, an
  enum and arrays of each; [IR_COOKBOOK.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#typed-json)).
  Because the encoding is calls of the writer's methods, it is written in the
  writer's modes: a writer set with `setIndent(2)` encodes what
  `JSON.stringify(v, null, 2)` writes, and a `setStrict(true)` writer fails a
  NaN or infinite `f64` field with `JSON_WRITE_NON_FINITE`
  (`tests/link/std_json_writer`).
- **A key is sent to its field by its length, then by one byte.** The code
  written for a class of three or more fields switches on the key's length in
  bytes, so a key is compared only with the names of that length. Where three
  or more names share a length, it switches once more, on the key's byte at
  the one position where those names differ most, and calls `keyIs` for each
  name that has that byte there, in declaration order; a byte none of them has
  is an unknown key at once. One or two names, of a class or of one length,
  are compared in turn with `keyIs`, which is no more calls. A key with an escape has no byte to switch on there, and is compared
  with every name of its length, so `"\u0069d"` is the field `id`
  (`tests/link/std_json_typed`, "wide: every key escaped"). A key is
  therefore compared with the names of its length that share its byte at that
  position, usually one, rather than with every name in turn, and a field
  name that is not ASCII is dispatched by its UTF-8 bytes like any other
  ("names: escaped field names decode").
- **What a field may be.** `T` is a declared class, and every field of every
  class the call reaches is one of these; anything else is refused at the
  call's argument, naming the class and the field:

  | Field type | JSON | Decoded with | Encoded with |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `i32`, `u32`, `i64` | an integer written without a fraction or an exponent, in the type's range | `d.i32()`, `d.u32()`, `d.i64()` | `w.i32`, `w.u32`, `w.i64` |
  | `u64` | an integer written in digits alone, with no sign, fraction or exponent, up to 2^64 - 1 | `d.u64()`, through the tokenizer's `numberU64` | `jsonEncodeU64` |
  | a numeric `enum` `E` | the number of one of `E`'s members | `d.i32()`, then a `switch` over the members' values | `w.i32` |
  | `f64` (and `number` under `--number-mode f64`) | any number; past the double range an infinity, which the writer writes as `null` | `d.f64()` | `w.f64` |
  | `boolean` | `true`, `false` | `d.boolean()` | `w.boolean` |
  | `string`, `string \| null` | a string, and `null` for the second | `d.string(cur)` | `w.string`, `jsonEncodeStringOrNull` |
  | a declared class `C`, `C \| null` | an object, and `null` for the second | `C`'s own decoding, into the object the field holds | `C`'s own encoding |
  | `T[]`, `T[] \| null` for any of the above | an array, and `null` for the second | `d.i32Array(cur)` and its kin, or `C`'s or `E`'s decoding per element | `jsonEncodeI32Array` and its kin, or `C`'s or `E`'s encoding per element |
  | `Map<string, V>`, `Map<string, V> \| null`, for any `V` in this table, `\| null` or not, a `Map` included | an object whose keys are the map's, each value a `V`, and `null` for the second | the object's keys in order, each value decoded as a `V` and `set` | the map's entries in its order, each value encoded as a `V` |
  | `JsonNumber` from `nish/json-typed`, alone, `\| null`, in an array or as a `Map`'s value | any number, kept as the text it is written in | `d.number(n)`, which copies the number's bytes into `n` | `jsonEncodeNumber`, which writes them back |

  `` `jsonEncode` cannot handle `Sample.ratio`, which is `f32`: a field read or written as JSON is an `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `f64`, `boolean`, `string` or a declared class, an array of one of those, or a `string`, a class or an array with `| null` ``
  (NL2485, `tests/cases/json_reject_field_type`; two classes down through an
  array's element, `json_reject_nested_field`; in a `| null` field's class,
  `json_reject_nullable_field`; in a class a `Map` holds,
  `json_reject_map_value_class`; `i32[][]`, `json_reject_nested_array`, and
  `Level[][]`, `json_reject_enum_nested_array`; a generic class of the
  program's own, `json_reject_generic_field`). The message goes on to name the
  kinds added since: `` a `u64` and a numeric enum are too, alone or in an array, and so is a `Map` whose keys are `string` and whose values are any of these, with `| null` or not ``.
  A JSON object's keys are strings, so a `Map` keyed by anything else is
  refused, an enum included (`json_reject_map_key`, `json_reject_map_key_enum`),
  and so is a map whose values typed JSON cannot write, at any depth
  (`json_reject_map_value`, `json_reject_map_value_nested`). A `Set` and an
  array of maps are refused as well (`json_reject_set_field`,
  `json_reject_map_array`). An enum whose members are strings, or a mix of
  strings and numbers, is not one the language declares at all
  (NL1043, `json_reject_enum_string`, `json_reject_enum_mixed`), and a
  `const enum` is refused where it is declared (NL2285,
  `json_reject_const_enum`). A value that is not a declared class is
  `` `jsonEncode`'s value is `Point`, which is not a class: typed JSON reads and writes an object through the fields of a declared class, and an interface, a generic class or any other type is not one in this version ``
  (NL2486, `json_reject_interface`, `json_reject_not_class`). An interface is
  a record stored inline wherever it is held, and decoding into one is left
  for a later version. A call inside a generic function is checked for each
  class an instantiation binds (`json_reject_through_generic`).
- **Decoding is strict, and every outcome is a code.** The keys are the field
  names, byte for byte, or the names the class's options give them. Every
  field is required unless its class's options make it optional, each key may
  appear once, and
  a key that names no field is an error unless `d.ignoreUnknown` is set, when
  the key's value is stepped over, checked but not kept. The first error sets
  `d.failed` and `d.errorAt`, the byte offset of the token it was found at,
  and every later call does nothing, as the tokenizer's and the writer's
  errors do; `jsonDecode` answers `d.failed`, and `d.reset` starts over:

  | Outcome | Code | `errorAt` |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | a value of the wrong JSON type: a string for an `i32`, an array for a class, `null` for a field that is not `\| null`, a top-level value that is not an object, an integer that is no member's value for an enum | `JSON_DECODE_TYPE` (-20) | the value |
  | a number its field cannot hold: a fraction or an exponent for an integer, or out of range, a negative number (`-0` included) for a `u64` | `JSON_DECODE_RANGE` (-21) | the number |
  | a key that names no field | `JSON_DECODE_UNKNOWN` (-22) | the key |
  | a key given twice, a field's or a `Map`'s, however it is escaped | `JSON_DECODE_DUPLICATE` (-23) | the second |
  | a field the object does not give | `JSON_DECODE_MISSING` (-24) | the object's `}` |
  | more keys, over every `Map` field of the decoding, than `d.maxMapKeys` (4,096 unless set) | `JSON_DECODE_MAP_LIMIT` (-25) | the first key past it |
  | text that is not JSON, or that crosses a `JsonLimits` limit | the tokenizer's `JSON_TOK_ERR_*` (-1 to -13) | the tokenizer's |

  Nothing an input holds panics: the recursion is the data's, so the
  tokenizer's depth limit bounds it. That bound is the caller's
  `JsonLimits.maxDepth`, 128 by default: each level is one native frame, so a
  limit raised into the hundreds of thousands can run off the stack, and one
  kept to a few thousand cannot. The writer refuses a 65th open container
  (`JSON_WRITER_MAX_DEPTH`), so a value decoded from deeper than 64 levels
  encodes as `JSON_WRITE_TOO_DEEP` (`tests/link/std_json_typed`, which
  reaches each row at each depth, the limits included). A duplicate of a key
  `ignoreUnknown` steps over is not detected, because its value is never
  read. After an error every field of `out` holds a value of its type, some
  decoded and some as they were: an enum field or element never holds a
  number that is no member's, because such a number is not stored.
- **An enum is its number.** A numeric enum is read with `d.i32()`, so a
  number that is not an `i32` integer is that field's `JSON_DECODE_RANGE`, and
  an integer that is not the value of one of its members is
  `JSON_DECODE_TYPE`; a member's name, `"High"`, is a string and a type error
  too. Two members of one value are one number (`tests/link/std_json_typed`,
  "enum: two members of one value both read 1"). It is written as `w.i32` of
  its value, as `JSON.stringify` writes a TypeScript numeric enum.
- **A `u64` is exact to 2^64 - 1.** It is read through the tokenizer's
  `numberU64`, so `18446744073709551615` decodes and `18446744073709551616`,
  `-1`, `-0` and `1.5` are `JSON_DECODE_RANGE`. It is written as its digits,
  which `JSON.stringify` cannot do for a number past 2^53: `tests/run.js`
  holds `round-trip-kinds.txt` to `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(line))` with each
  integer past 2^53 kept as its own digits (`JSON.rawJSON`).
- **A class's options are one `static readonly json` literal.** A class
  gives a field another key on the wire, and lets a key be left out, in an
  object literal written in the class, which the compiler reads when it writes
  the class's code:

  ```typescript
  class Account {
    static readonly json = { rename: { userId: "user_id" }, optional: ["tags"] };
    userId: i32 = 0;
    tags: string[] | null = null;
  }
  ```

  `rename` maps a field to its key, a string literal of any bytes, so
  `{"user_id":7}` is decoded into `userId` and `userId` is encoded as
  `"user_id"`; the field's own name is then a key no field has. The key is
  dispatched by its length and bytes like any other, escapes and non-ASCII
  included (`tests/link/std_json_typed/options.ts`, "rename: escaped wire
  names decode"). `optional` lists fields whose key may be missing: a missing
  one sets the field to its initializer, on a fresh object and on one decoded
  into again, so a reused object does not keep what an earlier input gave it
  ("optional: sets the missing fields back to their initializers"), and
  allocates nothing to do it. Every other missing key is still
  `JSON_DECODE_MISSING`, and an optional key that is given is read like any
  other: once, and of its field's type. The member is not a field: it has no
  slot, the class's layout is what it would be without it, the program
  cannot read it, and a class without it is decoded exactly as before. It is
  the one `static` member a class may declare, and its options are checked
  where the class is declared, whether or not any call decodes the class,
  each misuse with its own code:

  | Misuse | Code | Case |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `static json` without `readonly` but with a type, `static readonly json` with a type annotation, or on a generic class | NL2492 | `json_reject_options_mutable_typed`, `json_reject_options_annotated`, `json_reject_options_generic`, and on a generic class nothing instantiates, `json_reject_options_generic_unused` |
  | options, `rename`, a key or an `optional` entry not written as the literal it must be: a module constant, an array for the object, a string for `optional`'s array | NL2493 | `json_reject_options_alias`, `json_reject_options_alias_whole`, `json_reject_options_not_object`, `json_reject_options_optional_not_array` |
  | an option other than `rename`, `optional` and `presence` | NL2494 | `json_reject_options_unknown` |
  | a name that is not one of the class's fields | NL2495 | `json_reject_options_misspelt_rename`, `json_reject_options_misspelt_optional` |
  | a rename to a value that is not a string | NL2496 | `json_reject_options_rename_number` |
  | two fields with one key, a rename to another field's own name included, or a field renamed or made optional twice | NL2497 | `json_reject_options_wire_collides`, `json_reject_options_wire_twice`, `json_reject_options_optional_twice` |
  | an optional field with no initializer | NL2498 | `json_reject_options_no_initializer` |
  | a rename to a key that is not valid UTF-8, a lone surrogate such as `"\ud800"` included, which no input could give | NL2499 | `json_reject_options_surrogate` |
  | `presence` or one of its entries not written as an object literal of string literals | NL2493 | `json_reject_presence_not_object`, `json_reject_presence_not_literal` |
  | `presence` naming a field, or a presence field, the class does not declare | NL2495 | `json_reject_presence_misspelt_field`, `json_reject_presence_misspelt_flag` |
  | a presence field that is not a `boolean`, is `readonly`, is the field it records, records two fields, is recorded by a presence field of its own or is renamed or made optional; a field recorded twice | NL2592 | `json_reject_presence_not_boolean`, `json_reject_presence_readonly`, `json_reject_presence_itself`, `json_reject_presence_shared`, `json_reject_presence_of_presence`, `json_reject_presence_recorded`, `json_reject_presence_renamed`, `json_reject_presence_optional`, `reject_json_presence_twice` |

  A spread or a computed key in the literal is refused by Phase 0 as it is
  anywhere (NL1061, NL1041; `reject_json_options_spread`,
  `json_reject_options_computed`), a subclass by `extends`
  (`json_reject_options_subclass`), and a second `static readonly json` is a
  duplicate member (`reject_json_options_twice`). The options are not a
  value: `User.json` names a class where a value is due, and is refused as
  any class name there is (`json_reject_options_read`). Only `static readonly json`
  may leave out its type: written `static json = { ... }`, or as an instance
  field, it is an ordinary field to the parser and needs one
  (`a type annotation is required`, `json_reject_options_mutable`,
  `json_reject_options_instance`), and an instance field called `json` with a
  type is an ordinary field, read and written under its own name
  (`tests/link/std_json_typed/options.ts`, "instance json: an ordinary field
  decodes"). The options are not a member, so a field or a method called
  `json` may come before or after them, as in TypeScript, whose statics have
  a namespace of their own ("order: a json field before the options
  decodes", "order: a json method before the options decodes"). Under Node the literal is a
  static property of the class that nothing reads.
- **`presence` records which keys were given.** A third option names, for a
  field, a `boolean` field of the same class that every decoding sets to
  whether the input gave that field's key; a key given `null` is given:

  ```typescript
  class UserPatch {
    static readonly json = { optional: ["email"], presence: { email: "hasEmail" } };
    email: string | null = null;
    hasEmail: boolean = false;
  }
  ```

  So `{}` leaves `hasEmail` false, and `{"email":null}` and `{"email":"a"}`
  set it true, which `optional` alone cannot tell apart from a key given the
  initializer. Any field may be recorded, of any kind the decoder takes and
  optional or not (`tests/link/json_presence`). The presence field is off the
  wire: no key decodes into it, `jsonEncode` leaves it out, it takes no part
  in the key-uniqueness rule, and no option renames it, makes it optional or
  records it. It is set when the object closes, from the per-field flag the
  decoder already keeps to report a duplicate or a missing key: one `store i1`
  per recorded field, no allocation, and a class that records nothing compiles
  to the code it did before. Each object decoded sets its own, so a nested
  class, an array element and a map's value answer for their own keys, and a
  second decoding into one object answers for its own input. A decoding that
  fails may have set some presence fields and not others (none, when the input
  is not an object), so they are read only after `JSON_DECODE_OK`. A JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) is applied with it: the patch
  is a class whose fields are all optional and recorded, and `null` on a field
  that is not `| null` is `JSON_DECODE_TYPE`, so the patch is refused before
  any of it is applied (`examples/merge-patch.ts`,
  `tests/link/json_merge_patch`).
- **A `JsonNumber` is a number's text.** `JsonNumber`, from `nish/json-typed`,
  holds a number as the bytes it was written in, so a field of it decodes and
  encodes any number byte for byte: an integer wider than a `u64`, a fraction
  with more digits than an `f64` holds, `1E+400` and `-0` alike
  (`tests/run.js` holds each line of `round-trip-options.txt` to
  `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(line))` with every number kept as its source).
  It is read as a number whole, not as an object, so anything but a number is
  `JSON_DECODE_TYPE`, and its length is bounded by `JsonLimits.maxNumberBytes`
  like any number's. Decoding into one reuses its bytes, so `Arena.used()`
  stays flat over decodes into one object. It reads its text as
  `nish/json-value` reads a number: `text()`, `isI64()` and `i64()`,
  `isU64()` and `u64()`, and `f64()`, the nearest double; `setText(t)` sets it
  when `t` is one JSON number and answers whether it was. A new one holds
  `0`. Its methods run under Node, and `tests/run.js` holds them to the
  native lines (`readers.ts`).
- **A `Map<string, V>` is an object.** Decoding empties the map the field
  holds once the object opens, then reads each key as a new string and its
  value as a `V`, made fresh for the key (a zero, `""`, the enum's first member,
  `null`, or a new object, array or map, which a `Map`'s value class is made
  with `new C()` for, so its constructor takes no parameters, NL2488,
  `json_reject_map_value_constructor`), and `set`s it, so the map's entries
  are the input's, in the input's order. A key the object gave already is
  `JSON_DECODE_DUPLICATE` before its value is read, whether it is spelled
  the same way or through an escape (docs/security/json.md, JSON-3). Encoding
  writes the entries in the map's own order, which is insertion order. That
  differs from a JavaScript object in one case: a key that reads as an array
  index (`"1"`) keeps its place, where `JSON.parse` would move it first
  ("map: a key like an index keeps the input's order"). Unlike the rest of a
  decode, a map's entries are made anew each time, so decoding into a map
  allocates its keys and values. A value whose read fails is not `set`, so a
  map never holds a value the input did not give ("map: and the map holds
  only the entry read before it"). The maps of one decoding take at most
  `d.maxMapKeys` keys between them, 4,096 unless set, the keys of a map inside
  another map included, and the key past it is `JSON_DECODE_MAP_LIMIT` before
  it is read ("map limit: one key past it: code", "map limit: 820 small maps,
  4,100 keys, are refused"); `d.reset` starts the count again. At `0` or below
  no map may take a key, and `{}` is the one map value accepted. The global
  `Map` hashes a string under a per-process random key, so a body cannot
  choose keys that collide, and this limit bounds what all the maps of one
  decoding hold together (docs/security/json.md, JSON-13).
- **Decoding reuses what `out` holds.** A nested object is decoded into the
  object its field holds, an array's elements into the elements it has, with
  new ones made past its end and the rest dropped, and a string field keeps
  its string when the input's is equal. So decoding one shape into one object
  again and again allocates nothing: `Arena.used()` is flat over 1,000 decodes
  of a three-level object (`tests/link/std_json_typed`). A string that changes
  is a new string, since strings are immutable, and only that: it is made by
  one `String.fromBytes`, straight from the input when the string has no
  escape and from its unescaped bytes when it has one, and those bytes are
  reclaimed at the call. A class the decoder has to make itself
  — an array's element past the end, or the object of a `| null` field that
  holds `null` — is made with `new C()`, so its constructor takes no
  parameters:
  `` `jsonDecode` makes a `Pet` with `new Pet()`, and its constructor takes 1 parameter(s): an array's element and a `| null` field's object are made by the decoder with no arguments, so their class's constructor takes none ``
  (NL2488, `json_reject_constructor`, `json_reject_constructor_nullable`).
  Decoding assigns every field, so a `readonly` one is refused:
  `` `Key.id` is `readonly`, and `jsonDecode` assigns every field of the class it decodes into ``
  (NL2487, `json_reject_readonly`). A decode stores what it makes into the
  object it fills, so a call inside a `using a = arena()` block is the NL2424
  of [that block](#using-a--arena) (`json_reject_arena_block`). An encoding only reads the object and keeps nothing, so it may run inside one (`tests/link/std_json_typed`). Two fields
  holding one object are decoded into it twice, the second winning.
- **Encoding is `JSON.stringify`'s text** for the same object, its keys in
  declaration order, which is also the order an object's keys come back in
  when it is decoded from text whose keys are in that order:
  `tests/run.js` holds each line of `tests/link/std_json_typed/round-trip.txt`,
  decoded and encoded natively, to `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(line))`. A full
  buffer is the writer's `JSON_WRITE_FULL`, and an object that holds itself
  ends at the writer's depth limit with `JSON_WRITE_TOO_DEEP`, because the
  encoding stops at the first failure rather than recursing on.
- **The TypeScript reading is class C**
  ([wp33-round-trip.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp33-round-trip.md) §2). Under Node the type
  arguments are erased, so there is no layout to write the code from, and the
  bodies in `std/json-typed.ts` that Node runs end the program with
  `panic("nish/json-typed: jsonDecode and jsonEncode are written by the compiler from the class's fields, and under Node the types are erased")`
  rather than guess a field's type from the value it holds
  (`tests/run.js`, "under Node, jsonDecode panics"). The translation is the
  code the compiler writes, written as TypeScript for each class: a function
  per class of the same calls into `JsonDecoder` and `JsonWriter`, which
  everything else in the module already runs under Node: `tests/run.js` runs
  the decoder's readers there and natively and holds both to the same lines
  (`tests/link/std_json_typed/readers.ts`). A program that
  imports `std/json-typed.ts` by path rather than as `nish/json-typed` is
  compiled as written and gets those bodies natively too.

## Capabilities

Each builtin's label is the `Capability:` line of its doc comment in [`runtime/nish.d.ts`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/runtime/nish.d.ts); the rules are here.

Every builtin carries exactly one **capability** label, or a deliberate none,
and the compiler works out which capabilities every function, module and
package can reach — directly, through any chain of calls, across packages — with
one witness call chain for each ([wp35-capabilities.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp35-capabilities.md)).
A program is refused for what it reaches only under a [capability
policy](#the-capability-policy); without one, the set is a report.

| Capability | Builtins |
| --- | --- |
| `clock` | `Date.now`, `monotonicNanos`, `wallClockNanos`, `statMtimeSync` (`tests/cases/caps_clock`) |
| `entropy` | `crypto.getRandomValues`, `Math.random` (`caps_entropy`) |
| `env` | `getenv`, `geteuid` (`caps_env`) |
| `exit` | `process.exit`, and `exit` from `nish:process` (`caps_exit`) |
| `ffi` | any call to a `declare function` (`caps_ffi`) |
| `fs.read` | `readFileSync`, `readFileSyncOrNull`, `readFileBytesSync`, `readdirSync`, `realpathSync`, `isDirectorySync`, `lstatOwnerModeSync`, `isExecutableSync` (`caps_fs_read`) |
| `fs.write` | `writeFileSync`, `appendFileSync`, `mkdirSync` (`caps_fs_write`), `writeFileBytesSync`, `renameSync`, `unlinkSync` (`caps_fs_replace`), `writeFileSyncMode`, `createFileExclusiveSync`, `mkdirSyncMode` (`caps_fs_mode`) |
| `net` | every `nish:net` export (`caps_net`) |
| `process.spawn` | `spawnSync`, `spawnSyncTo` (`caps_process_spawn`), `spawnPiped` (`caps_process_spawn_piped`), `spawn`, `kill`, `waitPid` (`caps_process_wait`), `setNice`, `setIdlePriority`, `setCpuAffinity` (`caps_process_nice`) |
| `signal` | `signalFd`, `readSignal` (`caps_signal`) |
| `tty` | every `nish:term` export (`caps_tty`) |
| `unsafe` | the six `nish:unsafe` exports: `uncheckedGet`, `uncheckedSet`, `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub`, `wrappingMul`, `readCString` (`tests/link/caps_policy_deny_unsafe`; "capabilities: each of the six `nish:unsafe` exports carries `unsafe` at its call") |

Everything else is none: printing (`console.*`, `write`, `writeError`, `writeBytes`),
`process.argv`, `process.platform` and `process.arch`, `availableParallelism` and `totalMemory` (`caps_host`), `panic`, `Arena.*` and `arena()`,
`Math.*` other than `random`, the conversions, the constant-time builtins, `secureZero`, the
string, array, `Map` and `Set` surface, and `nish/threads` (`caps_pure`). A
`nish:` import carries the label of the builtin it renames.

- A function is judged **per instantiation**: `pick<i32, double>` and
  `pick<string, firstLine>`, or `apply<lengthOf>` and `apply<(name) => ...>`,
  are separate entries with separate sets (`caps_generic`, `caps_fnarg`). A
  module's set is the union over its functions, a package's over its modules,
  and the program's is `main`'s closure (`tests/link/caps_package`). A
  parallel body cannot reach a capability at all: every builtin that carries one
  writes memory the runtime shares (`tests/link/caps_parallel`,
  `reject_caps_parallel_clock`).
- A program is **deterministic** when it reaches none of `clock`, `entropy`,
  `env`, `ffi`, `fs.read`, `fs.write`, `net`, `process.spawn` and `tty`: the
  same argv and stdin then give the same output. `tty` is among them although
  stdin is an input a deterministic program may read, because `nish:term` reads
  it against the clock (`waitStdin`'s timeout, `readStdin`'s "nothing yet")
  and asks the terminal itself. `exit` and `signal` keep a program
  deterministic (`caps_exit`, `caps_signal`).
- `--emit-capabilities <file.json>` writes the report: version, entry,
  `deterministic`, the program's set, then each package, module and exported
  function (and every instantiation of one) with its set and a witness chain
  per capability, `{ "function", "at": "path:line:col", "calls" }` per call,
  and then its `"panics"`: every [panic site](semantics-decisions.md#panic-sites) the function has,
  `{ "kind", "at": "path:line:col" }` followed by the keys `--emit-panics`
  writes after its position (`"proven"`, `"callee"`, `"via"`, `"allowed"`).
  Keys are in a fixed order, sets in the order of the table above, packages,
  modules and functions sorted, and every path relative to the entry's
  directory, so the file is byte-stable and diffable (`.caps.json` beside each
  `caps_*` case). `nish run --capabilities` — or `--capabilities` on a compile —
  prints one line on stderr, `capabilities: fs.read (not deterministic)` or
  `capabilities: none (deterministic)`, before the program runs, and leaves its
  stdout alone. `--emit-capabilities` without a file is a usage error, exit 2,
  and so is either flag with `--emit-ast`, which stops before the checker;
  with `--emit-checked` both are answered beside the dump, and
  `--fix`, which answers before the program is analysed, takes neither. `nish run` refuses
  `--emit-capabilities` as it refuses every product it keeps to itself.

### The capability policy

`--allow <cap>[,<cap>...]` and `--deny <cap>[,<cap>...]`, each repeatable,
and `"nish": { "capabilities": { "allow": [...], "deny": [...] } }` in the
root `package.json` (the one nearest above the entry, where `noPanic` is read)
are a **capability policy**, and a program whose entry reaches a capability
the policy does not grant is refused
([wp36-capability-policy.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp36-capability-policy.md)). The same object's
`dependencies` key grants a dependency its gated capabilities, as [a
dependency's capabilities](#a-dependencys-capabilities) says (NL3041, NL3042):

```text
main.ts:6:36: error: `main` reaches `net`, which the capability policy does not grant (the root package's `deny`); the chain that reaches it: main.ts:6:36 calls dial, client.ts:5:10 calls netAddress
```

- A denied capability is refused when it is reached. Giving `--allow` or an
  `allow` list makes the policy an allowlist: a reached capability it does not
  list is refused, `exit` and `signal` included. The command line can only
  narrow the manifest: denials union and allowlists intersect.
- What is judged is every function outside code can call: `main` alone in a
  closed `--link` build or under `nish run`, and in an open one (`-o` alone, a
  sidecar, a `declare function`, wasm) `main` and every exported function of
  every module, or every function at all under `--no-strict-exports`
  (`tests/wordings/nl2459_policy_library`, `nl2459_policy_unexported`). Each
  refused capability is one error (NL2459), reported in source order, spanned
  at the first call of the witness chain and naming every hop of it as
  `--emit-capabilities` writes them (`tests/wordings/nl2459_policy_deny`,
  `nl2459_policy_allowlist`; `tests/link/caps_policy_manifest`,
  `caps_policy_two_denied`). The command line can only narrow
  (`caps_policy_cli_cannot_widen`, `caps_policy_allow_intersect`,
  `caps_policy_allow_narrowed`, `caps_policy_manifest_allow_cli_deny`).
- `unsafe` can be denied — `--deny unsafe` refuses a program that reaches a
  `nish:unsafe` export anywhere in its closure
  (`tests/link/caps_policy_deny_unsafe`) — and never allowed: the import is
  the opt-in, so an allowlist does not refuse it and `--allow unsafe` is a
  usage error.
- `unsafe` travels like every other capability — to each caller, however far
  up, and to the module and package above it, including a dependency that
  imports `nish:unsafe` when the entry package does not — and keeps a program
  deterministic ("capabilities: `unsafe` reaches a caller two frames up, with
  the whole chain as its witness", "capabilities: a dependency that imports
  `nish:unsafe` gives `unsafe` to its package and to the entry that calls
  it"). No flag turns a check off for a whole program, so `nish:unsafe` is
  the only way to one and `--deny unsafe` sees every unchecked site.
- A name that is no capability, `--allow unsafe`, a capability both allowed
  and denied, and a directory scope (`fs.read=<dir>`) without `--sandbox`,
  which alone enforces one (**Directory scopes** under
  [The sandbox](#the-sandbox)), are usage errors, exit 2. In `package.json` they are errors where the
  manifest writes them: the wrong shape of `capabilities`, `allow` or `deny`
  written twice included (NL3032, `tests/link/caps_policy_manifest_shape`,
  `caps_policy_manifest_repeated`), a name that is no capability (NL3033,
  `caps_policy_manifest_unknown`), `unsafe` under `allow` (NL3034,
  `caps_policy_manifest_unsafe`) and a capability under both (NL3035,
  `caps_policy_manifest_both`).
- **The `"nish"` field is read strictly**, as [the no-panic scope](semantics-decisions.md#the-no-panic-scope) says:
  a key is decoded as `JSON.parse` decodes it, so a policy written with an
  escape is honoured (`caps_policy_manifest_escaped_policy`,
  `caps_policy_manifest_escaped_entry`), and anything the reader could
  otherwise not vouch for — a second `"nish"` or `capabilities`, a key other
  than `noPanic`, `capabilities` and `host` — is NL3036
  (`caps_policy_manifest_repeated_nish`, `caps_policy_manifest_repeated_policy`,
  `caps_policy_manifest_nish_unknown_key`).
- A policy changes no byte of the IR: a program inside it compiles and runs as
  it does with none (`tests/link/caps_policy_granted`,
  `caps_policy_manifest_granted`). `nish run` takes both flags and refuses
  before it links; `--fix` and `--emit-ast` refuse them.

#### A dependency's capabilities

A dependency — a package loaded from `node_modules` — may reach `ffi`,
`fs.read`, `fs.write`, `net`, `process.spawn` and `unsafe`, the **gated**
capabilities, only when the root
`package.json` grants them to it by name; it reaches every other capability
without one ([wp40-dependency-capabilities.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp40-dependency-capabilities.md)):

```json
{ "nish": { "capabilities": { "dependencies": { "pkg_http": ["net"] } } } }
```

A dependency that reaches one it is not granted is refused (NL2576), in the
dependency, naming the package, the capability and the function:

```text
node_modules/pkg_http/src/index.ts:6:10: error: the dependency `pkg_http` reaches `net` through `dial`, which the root package does not grant it; grant it with "nish": { "capabilities": { "dependencies": { "pkg_http": ["net"] } } } — the chain that reaches it: node_modules/pkg_http/src/index.ts:6:10 calls netAddress
```

- A dependency's capabilities are the union over **every** function its
  modules define, exported or not, called or not
  (`tests/link/caps_dep_unexported`), and what it reaches through another
  dependency is its own: granting the package that dials refuses the one that
  calls it (`caps_dep_transitive`). One error per package and capability,
  spanned at the first call of the witness chain from the package's first
  function, in source order, that reaches it (`caps_dep_order`; one refused and
  one granted program per capability, `caps_dep_net_refused` …
  `caps_dep_unsafe_granted`).
- The standard library is never refused, and what decides is where a module
  was resolved, not its package's name: a dependency that calls itself `nish`
  is judged like any other (`caps_dep_std_not_refused`, `caps_dep_named_nish`).
  The ungated capabilities need no grant (`caps_dep_ungated`).
- A function argument counts where it is instantiated: the root's function
  passed to a dependency's template makes the instantiation, which is the
  dependency's, reach what that function reaches, so the dependency is
  refused for it (`caps_dep_fnarg_callback`).
- Only the root manifest grants: no flag does (`--allow net` leaves the
  dependency refused, `caps_dep_cli_cannot_grant`), nor the dependency's own
  manifest (`caps_dep_self_grant`), and a grant never widens the root's own
  policy — a capability the root denies is refused by NL2459 whoever is
  granted it (`caps_dep_root_deny_wins`).
- `dependencies` is read as strictly as the rest of the field: a value that is
  not an object, a package named twice, a grant that is not an array and an
  entry that is not a string are NL3041 (`caps_dep_manifest_not_object`,
  `_repeated`, `_not_array`, `_non_string`), a name that is no capability is
  NL3033 (`caps_dep_manifest_unknown`) and one that is not gated NL3042
  (`caps_dep_manifest_ungated`). `unsafe` may be granted, keys are decoded as
  JSON, and a grant to a package the program does not load is no error
  (`caps_dep_manifest_unsafe`, `_escaped_name`, `_unloaded`).
- `fs.read` and `fs.write` are gated: a dependency that reads or writes a file
  needs its grant like one that dials (`caps_dep_fs_read_refused`,
  `caps_dep_fs_write_refused`).

A grant entry may carry an **argument**, `capability=argument`, which narrows
it: a directory for `fs.read` and `fs.write`, a program for `process.spawn`,
a numeric host, or a Unix socket's absolute path, for `net`. An entry
without one grants the capability whole, as before:

```json
{ "nish": { "capabilities": { "dependencies": {
  "pkg_tool": ["fs.read=./data", "process.spawn=git", "net=127.0.0.1"]
} } } }
```

- A directory is resolved from the root package's directory and must exist
  when the program is built (NL3047); a program is found on `PATH`, or as a
  path from that directory (NL3046); a host is an IPv4 or IPv6 address, the
  form `nish:net` takes (NL3045). `ffi`, `unsafe` and the ungated
  capabilities take no argument (NL3048; all four in
  `caps_dep_manifest_arg_refused`). A capability may be named more than once,
  one argument each.
- What the compiler can see it checks: a string literal a dependency hands
  `readFileSync`, `writeFileSync`, `spawnSync` or `netAddress` outside its
  grant is refused (NL2594), at the literal:

  ```text
  node_modules/pkg_conf/src/index.ts:2:38: error: the dependency `pkg_conf` hands `readFileSync` "/etc/passwd", which its `fs.read` grant does not cover: it is granted fs.read=data; name it in the grant, or grant `fs.read` whole
  ```

  (`caps_dep_arg_fs_too_narrow`, `_spawn_too_narrow`, `_net_too_narrow`; the
  grant that covers each, `caps_dep_arg_granted`).
- What it cannot see — a computed path, program or host — the build leaves to
  `--sandbox`, which scopes Landlock to the granted directories and
  programs ([The sandbox](#the-sandbox), `tests/link/sandbox_dep_*`).
  Hosts have no run-time check: seccomp cannot read the address a socket is
  given, so a `net=<host>` grant binds only the literals the build sees.
- The lockfile records the arguments (`"pkg_conf": ["fs.read=data"]`). A
  grant past them — a new directory, program or host for a capability the
  row records narrowed — is NL2593 until the lock is updated; a row that
  records the capability whole accepts any argument (`caps_lock_args`).
- `@nish_sandbox` takes a fifth operand for the programs a
  `process.spawn=<program>` grant allows, null when none is named:
  `call void @nish_sandbox(i32 32, i32 1, i8* null, i8* null, i8* null)`.
  The four-operand call in "The sandbox" below predates it.

#### The capability lockfile

`--update-capability-lock` writes `nish-capabilities.lock.json` beside the
nearest `package.json` above the entry (beside the entry when there is none),
recording every capability each dependency reaches, gated or not. While the
file exists, every build is held to it:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "packages": {
    "pkg_http": ["net"]
  }
}
```

A dependency that reaches a capability its row does not record is refused
(NL2577), in the dependency, with the same witness chain as NL2576:

```text
node_modules/pkg_http/src/index.ts:6:10: error: the dependency `pkg_http` reaches `net` through `dial`, which `nish-capabilities.lock.json` does not record for it; review the chain, then record it with `--update-capability-lock` — the chain that reaches it: node_modules/pkg_http/src/index.ts:6:10 calls netAddress
```

- Only growth is an error. A row that records more than the dependency
  reaches, or a row for a package the program no longer loads, is accepted
  (`tests/link/caps_lock_shrink`, `caps_lock_stale`); a dependency with no row
  is held to an empty one (`caps_lock_no_row`, `caps_lock_no_row_pure`). One
  error per package and capability, in NL2576's order (`caps_lock_growth`).
- The comparison runs after both policies: a build the root's policy or the
  dependency grants refuse is refused by them, and `--update-capability-lock`
  on it writes nothing (`caps_lock_refused`). The flag skips the comparison and
  rewrites the file, even a malformed one.
- The file is byte-stable: packages sorted, capabilities in the fixed order of
  the report, two-space indentation, one trailing newline, `[]` for a package
  that reaches nothing. Neither the standard library nor the root package has
  a row.
- It is read strictly: text that is not JSON, a `version` other than `1`, a key
  other than `version` and `packages`, a name that is no capability, and a key
  or capability written twice are NL3043, spanned in the lockfile
  (`caps_lock_bad_json`, `_version`, `_key`, `_capability`, `_repeated`).
- The lockfile changes no byte of the IR. `nish run` takes the flag, and checks
  the program against the file before it looks in its cache, so the file is not
  part of the cache key and a cache hit is held to it too. `--fix` and
  `--emit-ast` refuse the flag.

### The sandbox

`--sandbox` holds a running native program to the capabilities its `main`
reaches. The policy above refuses at compile time a program that reaches more
than it grants; the sandbox makes the kernel refuse, at run time, what the
program's code does not reach, `ffi` callees and constructors included
([wp37-os-sandbox.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp37-os-sandbox.md),
[security/sandbox.md](../../security/sandbox.md)):

```llvm
@.sandbox.preinit = internal constant void ()* @.sandbox.apply, section ".preinit_array", align 8
@llvm.used = appending global [1 x i8*] [i8* bitcast (void ()** @.sandbox.preinit to i8*)], section "llvm.metadata"

define internal void @.sandbox.apply() {
entry:
  call void @nish_sandbox(i32 0, i32 1, i8* null, i8* null)
  ret void
}

define noundef i32 @main(i32 noundef %argc, i8** noundef %argv) #1 {
entry:
  call void @nish_sandbox_check()
```

- **The flag.** `--sandbox` is strict; `--sandbox=best-effort` runs on a
  kernel that lacks part of the confinement and says in one line on stderr
  what it could not withhold. Any other mode is a usage error, exit 2. It is
  accepted by `--link`, by `nish run` (before the file) and on the IR-only
  route, alone or beside the flags that write a file next to the IR; the
  `.ll` then carries the call, and linking it by hand keeps the confinement
  (`tests/cases/sandbox_hello`). `--emit-ast`, `--emit-checked`, `--emit-ts`,
  `--fix`, `--emit-napi` and `--emit-napi-async` refuse it, exit 2, since none
  writes a program with a `main` to confine, and so does an entry module that
  declares no `main` and holds no [top-level code](declarations.md#top-level-code) to run
  as one (`--sandbox` on a script confines the `main` its code becomes). `--sandbox` and `--sandbox=best-effort` on one command
  line are refused, exit 2; the same one twice is one.
- **The call.** The first operand is `main`'s capability mask, numbered as
  `--emit-capabilities` numbers the bits (`clock` 0 … `tty` 10, `unsafe` 11), the
  second `1` for strict and `2` for best-effort; the two `i8*` operands are
  the `fs.read` and `fs.write` directory scopes below, `null` when there are
  none. `nish_sandbox` runs from `.preinit_array`, after the loader and
  before any constructor of the executable, an `ffi` object or a shared
  library, and applies, in order: `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS`, a drop of every
  Linux capability (each set read back), a Landlock ruleset masked to the ABI
  the kernel answers, and a seccomp filter. `main` calls
  `nish_sandbox_check` first, which refuses to run a program whose C library
  never ran `.preinit_array` (musl), with exit 126 and one line: `nish:
  --sandbox: the C library did not run .preinit_array, so the program was
  not confined`.
- **What each capability's absence withholds.** Without `fs.read`, Landlock
  withholds reading files and directories; without `fs.write`, writing,
  making, removing, renaming and linking (within one directory too) and
  truncating, and seccomp
  answers `EPERM` to `chmod`, `chown`, `utimensat`, `setxattr` and their
  siblings, which Landlock does not decide. Without `process.spawn`,
  `execve`, `execveat`, `fork`, `vfork` and a `clone` without
  `CLONE_THREAD` kill the process, `clone3` answers `ENOSYS`, and Landlock
  withholds executing files and device `ioctl`s (ABI 5); with it, executing
  and reading files and device `ioctl`s are granted beneath `/`, since a
  child must load its binary and libraries, so a program that reaches
  `process.spawn` can read any file the user can whether or not it reaches
  `fs.read`. Without `net`, `socket`, `socketpair`, `connect`,
  `bind`, `listen`, `accept` and `accept4` kill it. With `net` but without
  `fs.write`, a pathname `unixListen` or `unixListenMode` is **`-13`**:
  Landlock counts making the socket file as a write (`MAKE_SOCK`), while an
  abstract name binds. The sandbox uses no Landlock right that covers
  connecting to a pathname socket, so `net` alone still lets `unixConnect`
  reach any pathname listener whose file and directories the user may
  reach; only abstract
  names outside the sandbox are scoped, from ABI 6. `ffi`, `unsafe`, `tty`,
  `clock`, `entropy`, `env`, `exit` and `signal` withhold nothing of their
  own; the ABI 6 scopes under **Always** apply whatever `main` reaches.
- **Directory scopes.** Under `--sandbox`, `--allow fs.read=<dir>` and
  `--allow fs.write=<dir>` grant the capability beneath `<dir>` alone. The
  directory is resolved, symlinks and all, when the program is built, and
  must exist then, or it is a usage error, exit 2: `` compile:
  `fs.read=<dir>` names no directory; a scope is a directory that exists when
  the program is built ``. Any other capability scoped, or a scope in
  `--deny`, is refused, exit 2, and so is a scope without `--sandbox`, as
  before. A scope narrows the policy like any `--allow` list, so the same
  list names every other capability the program reaches. A capability also
  granted whole is granted whole. The scopes are emitted as one constant per
  capability, each directory ended by a NUL and the list by a second:
  `@.sandbox.read = private unnamed_addr constant [N x i8] c"/srv/data\00\00"`,
  passed as `nish_sandbox`'s third (`fs.read`) and fourth (`fs.write`)
  operand, `null` when `main` does not reach the capability. Landlock grants
  the scoped access beneath each directory and nothing else, except that a
  `main` reaching `process.spawn` keeps reading every file beneath `/`
  (`READ_FILE`, so that `exec` can load a program), scope or not; `chmod`,
  `chown`, `utimensat`, `setxattr` and their siblings still answer `EPERM`
  inside an `fs.write` scope, since seccomp cannot read a path. A main that
  reaches `ffi` is widened by the policy's `net`, `fs.read`, `fs.write` and
  `process.spawn` grants, a scope included, since foreign code reaches them
  without the checker seeing it. A directory cannot hold a comma.
- **The CPU count.** Before it confines anything, `nish_sandbox` reads the
  CPU count (the affinity mask and the cgroup quota) and keeps it as the
  thread pool's ceiling, since without `fs.read` the quota under
  `/sys/fs/cgroup` cannot be read afterwards. `NISH_NUM_THREADS` still lowers
  the pool. `availableParallelism()` reads the count again on each call and
  is not bounded by that ceiling, so in such a program it no longer sees the
  quota.
- **Always.** `ptrace`, `process_vm_readv`, `process_vm_writev` and
  `pidfd_getfd` kill; io_uring kills unless both `net` and `process.spawn`
  are granted; on x86-64 a system call numbered with bit 30 (x32) kills, and
  a call from any other architecture's entry kills. A killed process ends by
  `SIGSYS`, exit status 159 from a shell. From Landlock ABI 6 a sandboxed
  process cannot signal or reach the abstract sockets of a process outside
  it.
- **Refusals.** A program whose sandbox cannot be applied prints one line,
  `nish: --sandbox: ...`, and exits 126 before `main` runs. Strict refuses a
  kernel without Landlock, and one below ABI 3 when `fs.write` is not
  granted, since `TRUNCATE` cannot be withheld there, or when it is granted
  only beneath a directory, since below ABI 3 that grants nothing beneath
  `/`; best-effort runs on
  both, naming what it could not withhold (without Landlock, files are not
  confined at all). A scope directory missing at run time is refused by
  strict, `nish: --sandbox: cannot open the directory <dir> (ENOENT)`;
  best-effort leaves its rule out, so nothing beneath it is granted, and
  names it once. Neither mode refuses a kernel without `IOCTL_DEV` (ABI 5)
  or the signal and socket scopes (ABI 6); best-effort names them.
- **Targets.** A darwin target, given or the host's, is refused (NL3044,
  `tests/wordings/nl3044_sandbox_darwin`). The wasm and WASI targets
  (`wasm32`, `wasm32-wasi`) accept the flag
  and emit no call, since the host already holds a module to its imports;
  `--profile wasm` refuses IR built with `--sandbox` for the host. A `.ll`
  built with `--sandbox` and linked on a platform other than Linux refuses to
  run, exit 126.
- **No byte of a program's IR moves without the flag**: the entry, its
  `@llvm.used` slot and the two declarations are emitted only under
  `--sandbox` ("sandbox: without the flag the IR is the sandboxed IR less the
  sandbox's lines"). `--runtime-decls`, which lists every declaration the
  runtime answers, lists the two whatever the flag.
- **Reserved names.** The runtime calls `prctl` and `syscall` from C, so in
  every build, sandboxed or not, a `declare function` of either name is
  refused as a reserved C symbol (NL3037).
